cs.CV · cs.AI
large language model
大语言模型相关
Abstract
Long video understanding remains a daunting challenge for existing multimodal large language models (MLLMs), mainly due to the large number of visual tokens accumulated in long videos. Currently, frame selection and token selection are two main paradigms for addressing this issue, both aiming to select relevant visual information to form a compact input for MLLMs. A natural approach combines these two paradigms by selecting frames before pruning tokens, but noisy frame-level relevance estimates can cause irreversible evidence loss. In this paper, we study this problem from the perspective of assessing the spatiotemporal distribution of query-specific evidence and propose a novel and training-free approach termed NULLTOK. For every patch across all frames, we construct an empirical-null distribution from 64 group-matched irrelevant control queries, capturing the scores expected in the absence of target-specific evidence. Target affinities are calibrated against these same-position references into right-tail Monte Carlo p-values, which are discrete super-uniform under a conditional exchangeability assumption. Calibrated screening and a high-recall semantic guard produce candidate tokens for deterministic visual deduplication and joint spatiotemporal budget allocation. To validate NullTok, we apply it to two representative MLLMs and conduct extensive experiments on a set of video benchmarks. The experimental results demonstrate its effectiveness under a bounded visual token budget. For example, it achieves 65.81% and 68.85% on Video-MME using frozen LLaVA-Video-7B and Qwen3-VL-8B backbones, respectively, at a cap of 64 full-frame equivalents (FFE), without subtitles or audio. These results outperform all evaluated baselines on Video-MME under the same budget for both backbones. Code is available at https://github.com/potato-kitty/NullTok.

Dual-Manifold Variational Autoencoders
双流形变分自编码器
Hongxu Chen, Chun Wang, Yanghao Wang, Hongxiang Li, Zhen Wang, Zhixiang Zhang, Long Chen
cs.CV · cs.AI
diffusion
扩散模型相关
Abstract
In latent diffusion models, expanding the latent dimension of variational autoencoders (VAEs) is essential to push the upper bound of reconstruction quality. However, without explicit structural constraints, such unregularized expansion easily yields a rugged and ill-conditioned latent manifold, causing generated latents to drift off the manifold during generation (i.e., off-manifold problem). Recent works smooth this manifold by using external foundation models (e.g., DINOv2) as a topological regularizer. However, we argue that tying the latent space to frozen external priors inherently restricts generalization: bound by their pre-training distributions and semantic biases, they may fail to capture faithful visual details on out-of-distribution domains. Observing that low-dimensional latents naturally form a smoother, generation-friendly manifold, we propose dual-manifold VAE (DM-VAE) to leverage internal representations as a topological regularizer. Specifically, DM-VAE pairs a high-dimensional reconstructive branch with a low-dimensional branch that extracts a clean topological skeleton, anchoring the high-dimensional manifold to this smooth subspace. Building upon this framework, we further introduce topological representation alignment (TRA) to supervise intermediate generator features during training, and internal guidance with topological skeleton (IG_TS) to guide structural components while preserving high-frequency details at inference. On ImageNet-1K (256x256), our foundation-model-free DM-VAE achieves a state-of-the-art rFID of 0.12 and a generation FID50K of 1.28 (w/o CFG) and 1.20 (w/CFG), and further reaches 1.11 when orthogonally combined with DINOv2.

SpiderMark: Hybrid Watermarking for Generative AI via Algorithmic Injection and Learning-Based Verification
SpiderMark：通过算法注入与基于学习的验证实现面向生成式人工智能的混合水印
Chihcheng Hsieh, Yang Song, Flora Salim, Martin Bell, Jacinto C. Nascimento, Catarina Moreira
cs.CV · cs.AI
diffusion
扩散模型相关
Abstract
The proliferation of diffusion-based generative models has intensified the need for reliable methods to trace and verify the provenance of AI-generated images. Existing watermarking approaches for diffusion models typically rely on isotropic frequency patterns and handcrafted detection metrics, which are prone to directional vulnerability and threshold instability across diverse image transformations. We propose SpiderMark, a hybrid watermarking framework that combines algorithmic frequency-domain injection with learning-based probabilistic verification, requiring no modifications to pretrained diffusion model weights. SpiderMark embeds a structured spider-web pattern, comprising radial spokes and concentric polygonal rings, into the Fourier representation of the initial latent noise, and trains a lightweight ResNet-18 verifier augmented with auxiliary similarity cues (PSNR and L1) to produce a continuous watermark confidence score for watermark detection. Across nine evaluation conditions, SpiderMark achieves the highest fixed-threshold Accuracy in eight, while retaining strong detection on unseen COCO prompts without verifier retraining. CLIP similarity and FID measurements show that these detection gains are accompanied by small measured differences in prompt alignment and distributional image quality. SpiderMark establishes that structured watermark geometry and learned probabilistic verification can be unified into a single, practical framework, bridging the gap between imperceptibility, robustness, and real-world verifiability for generative AI content attribution.

ViLFlow: Parallel Vision-Language Generation with Continuous Latent Flows

cs.CV · cs.LG

Abstract
Vision-language generation has predominantly relied on autoregressive and discrete diffusion models. Autoregressive models generate tokens sequentially, while discrete diffusion models typically predict tokens independently within each denoising step. We propose ViLFlow (Vision-Language Flow), a continuous-flow vision-language model that combines joint modeling of output embeddings with parallel token decoding. ViLFlow adapts pretrained continuous language generation to visual question answering and image captioning through learned image guidance and prediction-aware token decoding. A visually adapted teacher provides image-guided predictions as additional denoising supervision. The denoiser learns to reproduce these predictions directly, retaining one image-conditioned prediction per generation step. We train the token decoder on denoiser predictions and paired reference text to improve the conversion of continuous outputs into words. The decoder can be adapted independently, improving answering and captioning without further denoiser training. For captioning, it also supplies text feedback during late denoising, allowing decoded words to inform subsequent refinement. ViLFlow outperforms autoregressive and masked-diffusion baselines by up to 8.46 percentage points on VQAv2 and 4.50 points on GQA without GQA training. On COCO Karpathy test, it improves CIDEr by 16.25 over masked diffusion and 17.81 over sampled autoregression.

Every Query Routes Itself: Accelerating Video Diffusion Transformers with Per-Query Routed Sparse Attention
每个查询自行路由：用逐查询路由稀疏注意力加速视频扩散 Transformer
Zhen Huang, Shuwei Li, Ruizhe Yao, Xinrui Chen, Danyi Liu, Haoyuan Liang, Zhiyu Ye, Qiuyan Sun, Bingwei Chen, Yiyuan Li, Xu Zhou, Haohuan Fu
cs.CV · cs.LG
diffusion
扩散模型相关
Abstract
Self-attention over long token sequences dominates the inference cost of video diffusion transformers. Clustering-based sparse attention clusters both queries and keys and lets all queries in a cluster share one selection of key clusters. We show that this sharing limits accuracy: with key clusters and density fixed, attention grows more accurate as the query clusters are refined, and is most accurate when each query selects on its own, which needs no query clustering at all. We therefore propose Per-Query Routed Sparse Attention (PQRS), a training-free method that clusters only keys, lets each query select its own key clusters, and compensates for the unselected ones with their centroids. Per-query selections leave no query tile with a shared key list, so PQRS traverses key clusters instead of queries, buckets queries with identical selections into dense tasks, and merges their partial results in one pass under a fixed softmax offset carried from the previous denoising step. On four text-to-video and image-to-video models from the Wan and HunyuanVideo families, PQRS is the fastest of all the sparse attention methods we evaluate and the closest to the dense output, reaching $28.9$ dB PSNR on Wan2.1-T2V and $35.4$ dB on HunyuanVideo at $1.66$--$2.10\times$ end-to-end speedup.

H3Remover：无需配对数据强化视频对象移除
Kangjie Chen, Xiangyu Li, Jinhao Deng, Dongbin Zhang, Chaoda Zheng, Shijia Chen, Yuqi Zhang, Choo Sin Wai, Boyi Sun, Puyi Wang, Yu Zhang, Xianming Liu, Boyang Wang
cs.CV · cs.AI
diffusion
扩散模型相关
Abstract
Pretrained video editors possess rich removal and completion priors, yet may retain targets or alter unrelated content. We present H3Remover, which reinforces MiniMax-H3 Base Ref2VA for video object removal without paired object-free training targets. To discourage superficial edits such as recoloring, a target-removal reward favors calibrated depth changes consistent with revealing farther content. To limit unintended scene changes, a background-geometry reward encourages preservation of relative depth ordering. To preserve background appearance without retaining unwanted shadows or reflections, an appearance reward constrains RGB changes in source-derived protected regions while exempting targets and estimated effects. Frozen HPSv3 complements these constraints with perceptual-quality feedback for synthesized content. Evaluation regions remain fixed across candidates, and DiffusionART optimizes LoRA adapters with the backbone frozen. Experiments show substantial reconstruction gains over original H3, with qualitative comparisons demonstrating more effective object removal and better preservation of surrounding scene content.

扩散模型相关
Abstract
Visualizing intermediate representations could help us inspect the reasoning steps underlying a model output. Unified multimodal models offer this opportunity by combining understanding and generation in one architecture. Their image generators can access representations formed while processing text. We introduce the V-lens, which uses this connection to visualize a chosen token's hidden state without training a decoder. Across four diffusion-based and two purely autoregressive unified models, the resulting images reveal key intermediate concepts that connect a question to its answer even when the concepts are never named explicitly. Controlled tests show how this content changes with context, token position, and depth. We then introduce lens tuning, which supervises selected hidden states with pictures through the V-lens. Across BAGEL, SenseNova-U1, and HunyuanImage-3.0, the rate of correct visualizations of pronoun referents rises from 2-11% to 86-94%. Surprisingly, such visual supervision also improves text answers without supervising the answer tokens directly. Code is available at https://github.com/multimodal-ai-lab/V-lens.

When Do LLMs Model the Right Target? Problem Formulation in High-Stakes Risk Prediction
大语言模型何时对正确的目标建模？高风险风险预测中的问题表述
Jennifer Zhang, Amanda Coston
cs.CY · cs.LG · stat.ME
large language model
大语言模型相关
Abstract
Generative AI is increasingly used to assist with data science tasks, yet fundamental questions remain about its ability to correctly formulate analytical problems. We investigate how well large language models (LLMs) can formulate prediction problems when developing models for high-stakes decision making. We focus on one particular challenge to validity: decision dependency, which arises when historical decisions affect observed outcomes. We evaluate this aspect of problem formulation in LLM-generated code and explanations across child-welfare, healthcare, and employment settings, using 11 models from OpenAI and Anthropic and seven prompt conditions. We assess whether the LLM-generated code implements a procedure appropriate for estimating the intended outcome under the study's assumptions and whether the explanation acknowledges decision dependency. We find that LLMs do not reliably address decision dependency without guidance in the prompt. When prompts specify the target, the assumption needed to estimate it, and the estimation procedure, target-aligned implementation reaches 99-100%. Among frontier models, a simple prompt description of how decisions affect outcomes appears sufficient to elicit target-aligned implementation. Some responses also acknowledge decision dependency without addressing it in their code. Our findings suggest that analysts should not rely on LLMs to correctly formulate prediction problems without explicit methodological guidance and careful review. We propose validity-centered guidelines for LLM-assisted predictive modeling, covering prompt formulation, validation of the target and estimation procedure, and identification of key assumptions. Establishing validity is a necessary early step in evaluating whether to deploy a predictive model in a high-stakes setting, but deployment requires weighing broader ethical, institutional, and practical considerations.

LEDGE: An Efficient Simulator for Distributed LLM Serving on Heterogeneous Edge Devices
LEDGE：一个用于异构边缘设备上分布式 LLM 服务的高效模拟器
Zihao Wang, Ye Tian, Tajana Rosing, Nalini Venkatasubramanian
cs.DC · cs.AI
large language model
大语言模型相关
Abstract
Evaluating distributed large language model (LLM) serving on heterogeneous edge devices requires exploring diverse model partitions, device placements, and network conditions, making repeated physical experiments costly. An efficient simulator for edge LLM serving must support diverse, fine-grained placement configurations, capture runtime behavior, and accurately predict execution times while keeping simulation overhead low. We present LEDGE, a lightweight simulator for fast, fine-grained evaluation of distributed LLM serving on heterogeneous edge devices without executing tensor operations. LEDGE constructs event graphs supporting non-uniform tensor and pipeline parallelism, estimates execution costs using reusable performance models calibrated from end-to-end measurements, and simulates shared-link contention. We evaluate LEDGE on a heterogeneous testbed of 10 Jetson and Raspberry Pi devices, covering 17 model--precision combinations across 4 LLM families. On Qwen deployments, LEDGE achieves request-level mean absolute percentage errors below 3.6% and a 135.3 times aggregate speedup over physical inference. Performance model calibrated on one LLM family yield 7.44% zero-shot end-to-end latency MAPE across three other families. Further simulations show how shared-link contention affects placement decisions and network topology constrains scaling. Across four edge environments, LEDGE completes 26,773 simulation runs in 83.8 minutes, enabling efficient exploration of deployment strategies under diverse resource conditions and serving objectives. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/gdfwj/LEDGE.

Who are you? The Personal Imitation Game
你是谁？个人模仿游戏
Muhammad Rizky Wellyanto, Hajara-Yasmin Isa, Kexin Xue, Vishal Ravichandran, Wenpeng Lu, Jerry O. Talton, Ranjitha Kumar
cs.HC · cs.AI · cs.CL
large language model
大语言模型相关
Abstract
Large Language Models (LLMs) now perform strongly on Alan Turing's 1950 Imitation Game, so we propose a harder challenge, the Personal Imitation Game, which asks whether a machine can replicate a specific individual in conversation rather than a generic human. Testing with 30 participants, we establish a human baseline and report the identity signals interrogators rely on: stylometric features, personality traits, and biographical facts. To demonstrate the framework, we design an LLM-based system that plays the game for one of the paper's authors, drawing on an autoethnographic dataset spanning ten years of personal digital communication. In a 20-person deception study, interrogators choose our system over the author's own friends in 7 of 10 rounds, and the author over our system in 13 of 20; neither rate is distinguishable from chance at this sample size. We consider design improvements, applications of personal AI agents, and implications for identity and privacy.

Can Programs Replace LLM Judges? Executable Program Judges for Scalable and Efficient Relevance Labeling

Eugene Agichtein, Charles L. A. Clarke, Kaustubh Dhole, William Stern
cs.IR · cs.CL
large language model
大语言模型相关
Abstract
Large language model (LLM) judges have become a common way to create large-scale relevance judgments for retrieval evaluation. However, each judgment requires a potentially expensive call to a frontier model, and the judgments are hard to interpret and may not be reproducible. In this paper, we ask whether an LLM can write a readable program for each topic that replaces its per-document judgments. To address these issues, we propose ExecJudges, a method for generating fast, inspectable and scalable judges for automatic relevance labeling. Specifically, ExecJudges uses a frontier LLM to turn assessment guidelines into executable programs, which rely only on lexical matching, standard NLP libraries like parsers, and pool statistics. An ExecJudges-L variant also uses examples of human labels if available. We evaluate ExecJudges on seven TREC collections by comparing the produced labels with trained NIST assessors, frontier LLM judges, and recently proposed per-topic classifiers. Our results show that ExecJudges agrees with NIST assessors at the level of the Claude Sonnet 5.5 LLM judges on TREC DL 2019-2021. With a small number of human labels per topic, the ExecJudges-L variant agrees with NIST more than per-topic classifiers with the same labels on all seven collections, and either exceeds the agreement of LLM judges provided the same labels or is within about 0.05 of it in Krippendorff's alpha. The labels rank the official TREC DL runs with Kendall's tau of 0.87 to 0.94, and writing the programs incurs a one-time cost of $0.17 to $0.49 per topic, with no additional costs for grading. Our results suggest that ExecJudges offers a reproducible, inspectable, efficient and cost-effective alternative to LLM judges for labeling deep result pools for system evaluation or ranking improvements.

QDA: Closed-Loop LLM Quantization Design with Agents

Xingyang Li, Tianlang Zhao, Song Han, Ligeng Zhu
cs.LG · cs.AI · cs.CL
large language model
大语言模型相关
Abstract
Post-training quantization is the standard way to serve large language models at low cost. However, the best quantization recipe differs across models and precisions. As a result, experts must redesign it for every new model, which is time-consuming and often sub-optimal. Fortunately, an LLM agent can take over this design by refining the recipe over rounds of building and evaluating candidates, so that more rounds lead to better recipes. However, evaluating one quantized reasoning model takes tens of GPU-hours, and combining methods from different codebases means porting each to the new architecture by hand. We present QDA, a system in which an agent designs the recipe for each model and precision. To make evaluation fast, QDA scores each candidate in minutes by its output KL divergence from the original model on reasoning traces that the agent never sees, and checks promising ones with long generations to catch failures such as repetition loops. To make building fast, QDA provides a library of public PTQ methods that are compatible with one another and with new model architectures. Across four reasoning models, QDA improves accuracy over the strongest public recipe by 0.9, 1.4 and 2.2 percentage points on average at W4A16, W4A8 and W3A16, using 64 GPU-hours per search. On the 320B-parameter MoE model GLM-5.3-Flash at NVFP4 W4A4, it recovers 98.3% of the FP8 model's accuracy, against 96.9% for the best vendor checkpoint. Every QDA checkpoint also runs on existing serving kernels with no inference overhead. We will release the library, the evaluator and the harness.

Incremental Roseland: Batch-wise Landmark Diffusion via Kernelized Sequential Karhunen--Loève Update
增量 Roseland：经由核化序列 Karhunen--Loève 更新的逐批地标扩散
Jeanie Schreiber
cs.LG · math.FA · math.NA
diffusion
扩散模型相关
Abstract
Landmark diffusion (Roseland) computes a diffusion-map-style spectral embedding from the singular value decomposition of a degree-normalized data-to-landmark kernel matrix, at a cost far below that of full diffusion maps. It assumes, however, that all data are available at once. We introduce incremental Roseland (iRoseland), which casts the landmark affinity as a row-growing matrix whose SVD can be updated with a kernelized Sequential Karhunen--Loève (SKL) scheme. Degre correction is handled by a first order expansion about a reference mean kernel row and so that the landmark-side eigenbasis may be recovered from a single landmark-by-landmark eigendecomposition at each step. The presented method requires only a single pass over the data and runs in bounded-memory with state independent of the number of points processed. A forgetting factor lets the method track drifting distributions, and a sample-size-invariant embedding keeps outputs comparable across time. Experiments show agreement with Roseland to round-off on stationary data, and accuracy that exceeds equal-memory Roseland by an order of magnitude on long streams. On drifting data, we observe large gains from forgetting with a window matched to the drift.

cs.LG / 59 / 2611.23617
Error accumulation in reverse diffusion with an imperfect score: beyond path-space analyses
不完美得分下逆向扩散中的误差累积：超越路径空间分析
George Giapitzakis, Ankur Moitra, Andrej Risteski, Dhruv Rohatgi
cs.LG · cs.DS · math.PR
diffusion
扩散模型相关
Abstract
Diffusion modeling is a popular method of sampling from a complex, high-dimensional distribution $p$ using learned approximations of its (noised) score functions. Generating a single sample requires simulating the reverse diffusion process, which requires many queries to the learned scores. Thus, a priori, the learning errors can easily compound. Indeed, in existing theoretical analyses, the sampling error (as measured in total variation distance to $p$) accumulates polynomially with the horizon of the stochastic process. This is a consequence of bounding the error of the output law by the error of the law of the entire reverse diffusion path. In this paper, we demonstrate that by circumventing the "path-space" analysis, the error accumulation of the diffusion sampler can be mitigated when $p$ satisfies a Poincaré inequality. Moreover, we achieve this result as a special case of a broader framework that applies to any distribution $p$, but relaxes the error metric from total variation distance to a weaker metric capturing all sample statistics that do not "witness" the multimodality of $p$. We then zoom out from analyzing the diffusion sampler to the information-theoretic question: given a learned score with some error bound, how accurately can we identify $p$? We show that, for any given bound on the Poincaré constant of $p$, the diffusion sampler already nearly achieves optimal total variation error.

Variable Length Diffuse Everything: Arbitrary Length Generative Modeling on Arbitrary State Spaces
可变长度扩散一切：在任意状态空间上的任意长度生成建模
Kevin Rojas, Felix X. -F. Ye, Molei Tao
cs.LG · stat.ML
diffusion
扩散模型相关
Abstract
Diffusion and flow-based generative models have achieved remarkable results across diverse applications, but most assume data of fixed-dimension/length. Meanwhile, real-world problems such as layout generation often involve variable-length, multimodal data, such as continuous bounding box coordinates paired with discrete types. Existing methods typically address variable length by padding data to a fixed size or by introducing specialized objectives to model lengths explicitly, adding complexity and limiting generality. We propose Variable Length Diffuse Everything (VL-DE), a simple and general framework for variable-length multimodal generation on arbitrary state spaces. Instead of padding, VL-DE handles variable length through an insertion-based mechanism grounded in a principled theoretical framework, yielding a tractable training objective. In addition, by utilizing the fact that VL-DE is based on a generator with an additive form, we develop a higher-order sampler by appropriately handling the time dependence. Extensive experiments on layout and molecule generation demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach.

FDM+: A Framework for Constrained Control of the 2D Radiative Transport Equation
FDM+：用于二维辐射输运方程约束控制的框架
Hualing Zhong, Shuai Wang, Hui Xie, Heng Yong
cs.LG · physics.comp-ph
diffusion
扩散模型相关
Abstract
Applying the frozen diffusion model (FDM) [29] to the constrained control of the 2D radiative transport equation presents several challenges. These include the dimensional difference between control variables and state functions, the resolution mismatch between traditional numerical solvers and deep learning models, and solution non-uniqueness. To address these obstacles, we propose a novel approach, FDM+, which includes three key improvements. Firstly, a decoupled prediction architecture is introduced to address the dimensional heterogeneity. Secondly, an efficient parameterization strategy resolves the resolution mismatch. Meanwhile, we derive a total error bound to analyze how the parameterization error and the model estimation error jointly affect the performance. Thirdly, the conditional distribution learned by the diffusion model is leveraged to perform design space exploration for multi-solution problems. A series of numerical experiments demonstrate that FDM+ outperforms existing methods in reconstruction accuracy and design flexibility.

cs.LG · cs.DC
diffusion
扩散模型相关
Abstract
The Gradient Noise Scale (GNS) metric measures the signal-to-noise ratio of gradients in stochastic gradient descent and, as shown by McCandlish et al. (2018), can be used to approximate the Critical Batch Size (CBS) during neural network training. Despite its appearance in technical reports of frontier models, no open dataset of GNS measurements across modern architectures exists, limiting systematic study of the metric. We close this gap by releasing OpenGNS, a dataset of more than 400 GNS measurement trajectories spanning three domains: image classification with ResNets, autoregressive language modeling with Generative Pre-trained Transformers (GPTs), and image synthesis with Diffusion Transformers (DiTs), covering models from 11M to 1B parameters trained under Maximal Update Parameterization (muP) with dense batch-size and learning-rate sweeps. Building on this dataset, we study how the GNS depends on hyperparameters, scale, and training progress, and how it relates to the CBS. We find that the GNS behaves as a consistent "temperature of training", remaining stable across model sizes under muP at equivalent loss, and our results suggest task-dependent biases in its relation to the CBS: a tendency to overestimate the CBS for classification and to underestimate it for generative tasks, consistent in direction across common CBS definitions. The dataset is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/olympique-marcel/OpenGNS

LLM-Assisted Multi-Fidelity Bayesian Optimization: Fusing Expert Knowledge with Numerical Data
LLM辅助的多保真度贝叶斯优化：融合专家知识与数值数据
Dongjun Han, Mingyu Lee, Ikjin Lee
cs.LG · cs.AI · cs.CE
large language model
大语言模型相关
Abstract
Multi-fidelity Bayesian optimization (MFBO) reduces engineering design cost by combining inexpensive low-fidelity (LF) models with a few accurate high-fidelity (HF) evaluations and sequentially selecting designs to evaluate. However, when HF data are scarce, the LF-HF discrepancy is difficult to learn from numerical data alone, especially when physics omitted in the LF model makes it design-dependent. Yet even without sufficient data, domain experts often know which physics the LF model omits and under which conditions its effect grows. Existing multi-fidelity (MF) models cannot use such qualitative knowledge directly, but large language models (LLMs) can interpret it and compare designs accordingly. The proposed LLM-Assisted MFBO adds a knowledge basis to the conventional MF model: from an expert description of the omitted physics, an LLM judges which of two designs requires the larger signed residual correction, and a pairwise Gaussian process converts these judgments into the basis. HF data calibrate its contribution and sign, so the knowledge is not trusted blindly. On a lithium-ion battery design problem, the proposed method reduced the regret area under the curve of conventional MFBO by 61%. Knowledge quality, rather than the choice of LLM, determined whether the search was accelerated, as shown by a controlled study that varied the two independently. A knowledge-level ablation further quantified the contribution of each knowledge statement. These results show that LLM-interpreted expert knowledge can complement numerical data as an information source in MFBO.

Probing Physics in Motion Diffusion Models Against Their Own Estimate
在运动扩散模型中对照其自身估计探查物理
Saeed Ghorbani
cs.LG · cs.CV · cs.GR
diffusion
扩散模型相关
Abstract
Recent studies report that video diffusion models "know more than they show": physical properties decode better from their activations than from their inputs or outputs. But a diffusion model computes its clean-sample estimate from those same activations, so such a comparison measures how easily a readout extracts the information. Whether the model hides anything is a separate question. We set out to find hidden physical knowledge in kinematic text-to-motion diffusion models, where the physics of every intermediate estimate can be computed exactly, and recorded every layer along the sampling trajectories of MDM (two checkpoints) and MotionDiffuse. Against the usual baselines the layers do look ahead of the model's own estimate on balance and flight. With every readout tuned the same way, the estimate closes the gap: for balance and flight, adding a layer gains at most 0.01, a size that a positive control shows we would detect. The fall rate of jumps is the one clear exception. Early in denoising, MDM's layers add about 0.08 in $R^2$ (up to 0.11 in a refit) that the estimate does not yet show, and the gain fades as sampling proceeds; on MotionDiffuse it is small and not robust. The estimate also flags floating samples without training, but aborting them saves under a tenth of the compute. In a video model, plausibility that linear probes miss in Wan 2.1's clean latent becomes readable after one fixed nonlinearity.

Abstract
During human cortical development, functional systems become increasingly differentiated. We asked whether improved reasoning in language models involves a comparable regional reorganization. Applying diffusion-map embedding, used to characterize cortical organization, to matched base and reasoning-trained models from three families, we found broadly preserved gradient profiles with localized changes within a contiguous layer span. Grafting weights from these spans into instruction-tuned hosts improved mathematical reasoning on average, with gains rising with region overlap, while retaining more previously solved problems than grafts elsewhere. Across training, the span formed gradually during the early rise in performance, and grafts from intermediate stages helped. Grafts shifted most hosts partly towards their donors' behaviour and sometimes improved on problems the donors failed; the same analysis located a transferable span in a medical model. Together, these findings identify a reasoning-related region whose weights improve reasoning with low interference in the host's existing mathematical competence.

Elysium: Simulation-Free Unbalanced Schrödinger Bridges

Zihan Wang, Jianzhe Li, Zhenyi Zhang, Peijie Zhou
cs.LG · cs.AI · q-bio.QM
diffusion
扩散模型相关
Abstract
Reconstructing cellular dynamics from snapshots is challenging because the destructive nature of single-cell measurements makes tracking the same cells over time impossible. Cellular dynamics are inherently stochastic and involve changes in population size through proliferation and apoptosis. Growth-based methods represent population change as a rate on the density, which does not assign exits and entries to individual cells. Unbalanced Schrödinger bridges model individual events, but neural solvers for killed diffusion bridges simulate trajectories during training. We introduce Elysium, a simulation-free solver that jointly learns state transition and mass change. Using a killed Brownian reference and its time reversal, Elysium constructs direct regression objectives from an optimal endpoint coupling and conditional bridge distributions, without simulating trajectories during training. We show that the minimizers of the expected training objectives recover the optimal unbalanced Schrödinger bridge. Empirically, Elysium reconstructs state transitions, population size, and event distributions on simulated benchmarks with known killed-diffusion ground truth, outperforming existing deterministic and bridge-based solvers. On single-cell time courses, it interpolates cell state distributions at unobserved time points, tracks population expansion and contraction, and captures biphasic drug-response dynamics.

Atomic MathReasoner: Instance-Level Composition of Atomic Reasoning Skills for Mathematical LLMs
Atomic MathReasoner：面向数学 LLMs 的原子推理技能的实例级组合
Jiashu Li, Tianyu Gao, Qinglong Liu, Jinping Wang, Ye Wei, Zhiqiang Gao
cs.LG
large language model
大语言模型相关
Abstract
Most existing approaches enhance mathematical reasoning in large language models (LLMs) as a monolithic capability, despite the fact that different mathematical problems require different reasoning skills. Recent work has explored a more fine-grained perspective by decomposing mathematical reasoning into atomic skills and developing specialized modules for individual capabilities. However, how to effectively utilize these atomic abilities remains underexplored. To address this challenge, we propose Atomic MathReasoner (AMR), an instance-level framework for composing atomic reasoning skills. AMR first trains a library of capability-specific LoRA experts and performs gradient-free optimization over held-out validation subsets to discover a diverse set of low-loss composition prototypes. It evaluates the preference of each prototype using the token-level negative log-likelihood of reference solutions, filters ambiguous assignments through a confidence margin, and distills the resulting pseudo-labels into a lightweight router. During inference, the router selects an appropriate composition prototype for each problem, enabling problem-specific utilization of atomic skills without costly online optimization. Experiments on the AtomicMath benchmark across general and mathematics-specialized LLMs demonstrate consistent improvements. On Qwen2.5-Math-Instruct-7B, AMR increases average field accuracy from 64.4% to 68.1% at Level 1 and from 59.3% to 63.7% at Level 2, while improving average logical reasoning performance from 39.4% to 46.8%. These results demonstrate that effectively composing specialized atomic skills provides a promising approach to strengthening mathematical reasoning in LLMs.

cs.LG · cs.AI
large language model
大语言模型相关
Abstract
Large language models (LLMs) are used to explain clinical prediction models, on the promise that they can say what a model computes, find its faults and even reveal new knowledge in it. We tested the three promises where the answers could be checked. From the International Stroke Trial we trained four kinds of model (logistic regression, explainable boosting machine, gradient-boosted trees, neural network) for two outcomes on patients randomised earlier, planted one flaw in each of 24 copies (an under-predicted subgroup, a reversed risk factor or an implausible step) and mixed them with the 8 clean models. GPT-6 Astra audited each model three times, blind, through a tool that only returned the model's predictions; the judging rules were committed before any run and applied by program. Its surrogate models, with a median of 128 terms, reproduced the audited models' log-odds with a mean $R^2$ of 0.976 (0.959 for an additive surrogate of 42 terms fitted by an analyst). It found the planted flaw in 69 of 72 runs (96%; 95% CI 80% to 99%); a script written for the purpose found all 24. It also reported many more problems: 60% of 1,089 checkable reports failed the pre-specified check against the model's average behaviour; post hoc, most of these were real but small steps, and 15% of the checkable reports were not found in the model. Of 601 unexpected relationships it read out of the clean models, 11% held in patients randomised later (random pairs 6%; a regression scan's shorter list of its strongest candidates, 28%); after a check on the training data, 33% against 30%. With query access alone, an LLM can describe a black-box model faithfully and find nearly every planted flaw, as a purpose-written script also did; its reports of problems must be checked on the model and its discoveries on data.

Incremental Speciation in Evolutionary Red Teaming of Large Language Models
大型语言模型进化红队测试中的增量物种形成
Onkar Shelar, Travis Desell
cs.NE
large language model
大语言模型相关
Abstract
Speciation maintains distinct subpopulations in evolutionary search through similarity-based grouping and species-aware parent selection. For text-based individuals, niches depend on both the compatibility representation and the assignment operator that turns pairwise relations into species. We examine this design space in black-box evolutionary red teaming of large language models, comparing embedding and natural language inference (NLI) dissimilarities under representative-based and density-based speciation. Offline calibration on a 3,139-prompt archive shows that MiniLM embedding dissimilarity ($d_E$) and DeBERTa-v3-small NLI non-entailment ($d_{\neg E}$) produce different species structures at the same nominal threshold. Even with pairwise edge density matched to MiniLM, NLI density connectivity forms a few concentrated, mixed-topic species, with substantially more off-topic membership. These structural differences persist online under a matched evaluation budget. The endpoint top-50 median fitness favors incremental DBSCAN over leader-follower, but bootstrap intervals from 10 runs include zero, providing no reliable evidence of an advantage. Semantic diversity among top prompts declines in every configuration, with no consistent method advantage. The clearest difference concerns high-fitness population occupancy: MiniLM incremental DBSCAN maintains mature niches across seed topics, whereas NLI incremental DBSCAN attains the same highest observed median fitness while concentrating high-fitness prompts in variants of a few seed topics. Thus, representation-dependent connectivity predicts population structure more consistently than endpoint fitness. Species count alone does not establish quality-diversity, and more species do not necessarily preserve semantically diverse high-fitness prompts.

Harvesting Expert-Parallel Bubbles for Fine-Tuning
利用专家并行气泡进行微调
Oana Balmau, Saurav Banka, Jiaxuan Chen, Anne-Marie Kermarrec, Ramya Narasimha Prabhu, Rafael Pires, Mathis Randl, Martijn de Vos
cs.OS · cs.AI · cs.DC
large language model
大语言模型相关
Abstract
GPUs are expensive, yet latency-critical large language model (LLM) inference leaves part of them idle. Colocation reclaims this capacity by running best-effort work, such as fine-tuning, alongside serving. Many leading LLMs now use a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture, which adds a new source of idle time. Under expert parallelism, MoE experts are spread across GPUs, and because the router sends uneven numbers of tokens to each GPU, lightly loaded GPUs wait for the most loaded one. Even after applying load balancing solutions, such bubbles still take 8--13% of prefill time. We present BubbleTea, the first colocation system that leverages expert-parallel bubbles for fine-tuning. Unlike existing colocation systems, which make one scheduling decision for all GPUs per forward pass, BubbleTea predicts each GPU's bubble at every layer from the router's token assignment, and fills it with short chunks of fine-tuning work that reuse the weights already loaded for serving. We also introduce compiler passes that automatically derive these chunks from the served LLM as-is, without porting each model architecture to a separate training engine. Our evaluation on three MoE models, served on four A100 GPUs, shows that fine-tuning throughput with BubbleTea is 1.9--6.2$\times$ faster than with LLMStation, a state-of-the-art colocation system. BubbleTea keeps p90 inference latency within 10% of serving alone in 50 of 63 workloads, compared to 44 for LLMStation. On bursty production traces, BubbleTea trains 3.3$\times$ faster than LLMStation and 14$\times$ faster than a stock trainer colocated under CUDA MPS, with p90 inference latency staying within 7% of serving alone.

Measuring and Charging for Retained Context in Long-Context LLM Services
长上下文 LLM 服务中保留上下文的度量与计费

cs.PF · cs.CL

大语言模型相关
Abstract
Long-context large language model (LLM) services charge for repeated context, yet billing weights need not reflect its contribution to answer quality. We present a three-layer framework separating content relevance, observable proxies and auditable positional weights. Context-ablation experiments show that relevance dominates position and that distance-decay families do not outperform a relevance-only baseline. A measured serving stack shows that cache hits reduce repeated-prefix compute cost by over two orders of magnitude at 65,536 tokens, while cold resends constrain sustainable discounts. Cross-provider measurements separate cache value from tokenisation and list-price differences. Calibrated simulations reduce the 99th percentile of session charges by 31-42%, although revenue-matched nonlinear tariffs achieve similar reductions and median charges increase. The framework provides a bounded per-token accounting rule and measured deployment constraints, rather than a validated utility estimator.

cs.RO · cs.LG
diffusion
扩散模型相关
Abstract
Vision-Language-Action models have demonstrated strong manipulation capabilities. A limitation of VLA models is that most manipulation datasets focus on parallel-jaw gripper systems, making transfer to multi-finger hands challenging, particularly as teleoperation datasets are harder to collect with multi-fingered robots. In this work, we study how to best adapt VLAs to dexterous hands by pairing supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with diffusion-steering reinforcement learning (DSRL). Using $π_{0.5}$ and a LEAP hand, we evaluate five fine-tuning recipes across two simulation tasks using only a handful of demonstrations. Our empirical analysis yields three key insights: (1) SFT success is poorly correlated with post-DSRL success, meaning the best SFT checkpoint is rarely the most effective to steer; (2) freezing the vision-language model (VLM) and tuning only the action expert produces the most steerable policy for both training and out-of-distribution placements; and (3) low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is the least steerable approach. Consequently, we recommend an adaptation recipe that freezes the VLM, fully trains the action expert, and eschews SFT rollout success as a checkpoint selection metric.

Option-GRPO: Hierarchical RL Against AI Slop in Code Generation for Unseen SDKs
Option-GRPO：面向未见 SDK 代码生成中 AI 低质内容的层次化强化学习
Prashank Kadam
cs.SE · cs.CL · cs.LG
large language model
大语言模型相关
Abstract
Large language models increasingly produce AI slop in generated code: verbose, redundant, non-idiomatic implementations that pass functional checks but bloat codebases. The problem compounds on SDKs released after the model's training cutoff, where the model has neither idiomatic priors nor compositional understanding. We present Option-GRPO, a hierarchical reinforcement learning framework that adapts a code LLM to an unseen SDK from its source code alone, without human-written usage examples or test cases, and that explicitly optimizes for both functional correctness and code elegance. Our key insight is that SDK source code contains compositional structure that defines a hierarchy of reusable code patterns (code options) which simultaneously serve as the building blocks of a curriculum and the action space for efficient policy optimization. We show that code options induce a valid semi-Markov decision process, give conditional bounds under which shorter option description length implies more concise and, in expectation, more API-efficient programs, and analyze under stated assumptions how the option hierarchy improves credit assignment by a factor of $\sqrt{T/K}$. Using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with execution-based rewards at each curriculum level, Option-GRPO discovers SDK idioms, composes them into patterns, and assembles patterns into complete programs. Experiments on 12 unseen SDKs with a 32B-parameter base model demonstrate 61.4% pass@1, outperforming flat GRPO by 8.7 points, ExploraCoder by 11.2 points, and ReCode by 6.3 points. Option-GRPO produces solutions that use 34.7% fewer API calls and are 27% shorter than flat-GRPO outputs while maintaining higher correctness, directly attacking the slop problem.

Reliability is a user-specific property of large language models
可靠性是大型语言模型的一种用户特定属性
Xingyu Zhao
cs.SE · cs.AI
large language model
大语言模型相关
Abstract
Public benchmarks support comparisons of large language model (LLM) capabilities, yet users can experience the same highly ranked model differently. Drawing on traditional software reliability, we argue that the reliability of an LLM service should be assessed for specified users and conditions of use. This requires more than a capability score: evaluation evidence must support a claim about failure during future operation. We distinguish testing to discover faults from testing to assess reliability and identify ten modelling considerations behind such claims. We propose a six-workstream research roadmap linking claim specification, dynamic operational profiles, graded outcomes and noisy judgements, local probabilistic robustness, interaction dependence, and statistical inference with reassessment. Local probabilistic robustness addresses the behavioural variation hidden when different concrete inputs are treated as the same task. Published findings and an illustrative customer-support example motivate the roadmap; its integrated validation remains an open research task. Reliability claims complement, but do not replace, separate safety and security arguments. Capability scores should therefore be complemented by versioned operational claims that state whose requirements are covered, under which conditions, and with what uncertainty.

Re-Testing LLM-Based C-to-Rust Translations Against Their Original C
对照原始C重新测试基于LLM的C到Rust翻译
Muhammad Hassnain
cs.SE
large language model
大语言模型相关
Abstract
Most C-to-Rust translators use large language models (LLMs), and each reports a success rate from its own correctness check. We survey 34 C-to-Rust translators that use LLMs. Only one reports testing its check, and eleven release the original C and their Rust in runnable form. We re-test all eleven. We run the C and the Rust on generated inputs, compare every output, and count a divergence only where the C has no undefined behavior. All eleven release defective translations: we find 160 defects, 93 of them outright errors on ordinary inputs. Their own checks accepted 86 defective translations. For 81 of them, the released check never compared the programs on an input that exposes the defect. For three of the other five, it ran one but compared only part of the output. A success rate is only as good as its check. Before counting a translation as a success, authors should compare every output with the C's on inputs the repair loop never saw, check that a verifier reaches its assertion, release exactly what the check accepted, and report how they tested the check.

Metadata-Driven AI: An Architectural Pattern for Sustainable Data Analysis with LLMs
元数据驱动的 AI：一种利用 LLM 进行可持续数据分析的架构模式
Renaud Pawlak, Armen Sulejmani, Jordi Cabot
cs.SE
large language model
大语言模型相关
Abstract
Large Language Models (LLMs) let users analyse data in natural language, either by giving the data to the model to read directly or by having the model generate code to process it. Both routes send the data, or fragments of it, to the model; both pay for inference on every run; and the code a model writes to answer a question is usually discarded once the question is answered. We present Metadata-Driven AI, an architectural pattern that keeps the data away from the model and turns each analysis into a reusable program. Only metadata (not the actual data) crosses a one-way inference boundary to the LLM. The program the LLM returns runs next to the data and is kept, so that inference is paid once per analysis rather than once per run. We describe the pattern together with a simple cost model, a measurement of how little information crosses the boundary on public datasets, and a benchmark showing that a small, locally hosted model can serve as the generator. We illustrate the pattern on three applications, each built on a different implementation of it: geospatial photovoltaic prospection over live public APIs, extraction of portfolio positions from bank statements, and a conversational assistant over smart-city dashboards.

cs.CR / 77 / 2611.23666
Rented Oscillations: Multi-Tenant Data Center Workload Synchronization Attacks and Mitigation
租用的振荡：多租户数据中心工作负载同步攻击与缓解
Zaint A. Alexakis, Li Zhou, S. Gokul Krishnan, Charalambos Konstantinou
eess.SY · cs.CR
large language model
大语言模型相关
Abstract
Multi-tenant data center (DC) facilities rent computing capacity on demand, placing controllable load within reach of anyone willing to pay for it. This paper considers a stealthy adversary who rents workstations and runs deliberately unoptimized large language model (LLM) training, synchronizing their consumption into large periodic oscillations while each workload remains individually indistinguishable from benign training. The periodicity of such workloads is characterized experimentally and used to model facility consumption, showing that oscillations emerge from the interaction of concurrent workloads, whether aligned by an adversary or arising naturally. A combined small- and large-signal assessment, under a hardware-grounded threat model whose feasibility is supported by experiments on a supercomputer, locates the oscillatory weak points of the network. MW-scale oscillations are shown to saturate the generators' control limiters, amplifying their effect, while Floquet analysis reveals a lightly damped mode emerging near the forcing frequency. To counter both origins, signal-energy-based detection and mitigation are proposed, the latter re-timing the workloads to minimize the facility's oscillatory energy. The approach is validated through power hardware-in-the-loop (PHIL) experiments and real-time simulations on a surrogate model of the Saudi Arabian transmission network.

PhysDial: Adapting Pretrained Video Models for PDE Simulation under Changing Physical Conditions
PhysDial：适配预训练视频模型以用于变化物理条件下的 PDE 模拟
Yilong Dai, Yiming Sun, Shengyu Chen, Jiaqi Gong, Xiaowei Jia, Runlong Yu
physics.flu-dyn · cs.AI
diffusion
扩散模型相关
Abstract
Simulating how physical systems respond to changing conditions is central to control, design, and scenario studies. To our knowledge, prior PDE foundation models have not been trained or evaluated on changes within trajectories. Our counterfactual test measures how far predictions move toward a changed solver branch from the same state. Models trained on fixed conditions follow changes only partly. A PDE foundation model given a condition input after pretraining barely responds. PhysDial adapts a pretrained video diffusion transformer to eight two-dimensional PDE families. Coefficients enter with the noise level, condition fields as reference frames, and equation text as a prompt. In Kolmogorov flow, switches within trajectories account for about 5% of the training samples. At matched compute, they halve the error after a change in forcing wavenumber or amplitude. A few trajectories at new amplitudes more than halve extrapolation error. Without physics pretraining, PhysDial matches or exceeds PDE foundation models under training conditions on two turbulent flows. At step 64 on the Kolmogorov test split, PhysDial has 1.07 times the solver's small-scale energy and Walrus 7.1 times. Our experiments suggest that a learned simulator uses a condition only as far as its training data make that condition necessary for prediction. Learning from trajectories that diverge under intervention can help scientific simulators predict what would happen if a system's forcing or parameters changed.

Geometry-bridge flow matching for blind rigid-motion correction in head cone-beam CT
用于头部锥形束CT盲刚性运动校正的几何桥流匹配
Sungho Yun, Seungryong Cho
physics.med-ph · cs.CL · cs.CV
diffusion
扩散模型相关
Abstract
Rigid motion of a patient head during head cone-beam CT (CBCT) scan can degrade image quality and complicate recovery of accurate anatomical structures from the measured projections. We present a 3D flow-matching prior approach that learns the image changes induced by motion. Its geometry-bridge connects motion-corrupted and motion-free Feldkamp-Davis-Kress (FDK) reconstructed images of the same source volume through progressively reduced simulated motion. The forward projector's geometry derivative supplies analytic velocity targets along this path. A plug-and-play loop encompasses the learned image updates together with spline-based pose estimation, conjugate-gradient data consistency, and image total-variation regularization. Both the refined image volume and the FDK reconstructed image volume at the estimated poses are evaluated. On simulated 360-view scans from 30 held-out CQ500 patients with nominal per-component motion amplitudes within 10 mm / 10 degrees, the framework achieved state-of-the-art image reconstruction quality and motion accuracy in comparison with other methos such as learned autofocus and diffusion-based joint reconstruction. Mean peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) reached 37.1 dB and mean detector-plane reprojection error (RPE) was 0.27 mm. With matched endpoints at the inference settings, the geometry bridge improved PSNR by 1.6 dB and reduced RPE by 33% relative to image-linear training. With 50 prior updates and coarse-to-fine motion estimation, total processing time averaged 9.1 minutes per patient on an RTX A6000.

In Situ Training of Optical Neural Networks by Coding Agents
由编码智能体对光学神经网络进行原位训练
Ilker Oguz, Colin Christian, Christophe Moser, Demetri Psaltis, Gordon Wetzstein
physics.optics · cs.AI · cs.LG
large language model
大语言模型相关
Abstract
Optical neural networks promise fast, energy-efficient computing, but every device departs from its design and must be trained with the hardware. In situ training relies on an expert-built calibrated digital model of each device or on gradient-free trial and error. Coding agents, large language models that write and run programs, have shown an emergent ability to understand and edit the weights of digital neural networks. Here we introduce optics as code, a method in which a coding agent trains an optical neural network from measurements alone, through a harness that returns camera images of its probes and requires a hypothesis per request. We discovered that the agent forms a physical understanding of the optics and reparametrizes the network with interpretable optical elements tuned on the hardware. It outperforms gradient-free methods in classification and image encoding, approaching backpropagation through a calibrated model at a fraction of the cost. Needing neither per-device calibration nor gradients through the hardware, and improving with more capable models, optics as code offers a practical route to large, scalable optical neural networks and a general tool for calibrating and optimizing optical experiments.

Abstract
Rubric-based reinforcement learning constructs rewards for aligning large language models with human preferences, typically by equally aggregating continuous scores that a judge assigns to individual criteria. However, scoring heterogeneity across criteria can distort candidate rankings. Existing work has focused on improving judges, learning criterion weights, or refining aggregation, whereas the interaction between scoring heterogeneity and ranking remains insufficiently understood. We formalize this heterogeneity as \emph{reward gain imbalance}: each criterion enters the aggregated reward with its own reward gain, the gap between its expected scores on satisfied and unsatisfied responses. Counterintuitively, our experiments show that removing this imbalance, even with ground-truth labels, lowers ranking accuracy. To explain this, we derive an exact decomposition of the reward difference between any two candidates into a base satisfaction signal, a reward gain imbalance term, and a residual term, showing that reward gain imbalance can attenuate or amplify the base signal, and finding that misrankings usually concentrate on pairs where it attenuates. Guided by this analysis, we propose the adaptive \textbf{D}ual-\textbf{C}enter \textbf{C}lipping aggregation (DCC), which bounds each criterion's contribution to the reward difference instead of simply removing the imbalance. Using only the scores of the current candidate group, it determines a clipping interval that imposes a common upper bound on per-criterion score differences between candidates, limiting the excessive influence of extreme scores while preserving continuous judgment information....

Diffusion Models are Provably Efficient Priors for Sparse Recovery
扩散模型是用于稀疏恢复的可证明高效先验
Ivan Lee, Xingyu Xu, Yuejie Chi
stat.ML · cs.IT · cs.LG · math.OC
diffusion
扩散模型相关
Abstract
Diffusion models have transformed generative modeling through their ability to capture and generate samples from complex data distributions. This success has spurred substantial interest in using pretrained diffusion models as expressive priors for highly ill-posed inverse problems in imaging and sensing. Despite strong empirical performance, theoretical understanding of this approach remains limited: existing guarantees are often asymptotic or entail prohibitive computational costs in the worst case. In this paper, we address this gap by studying sparse recovery from a small number of linear measurements, a classical problem in compressed sensing. We show that, given an accurate diffusion model capturing a sparsity-promoting Bernoulli-Gaussian prior, a likelihood-guided annealed Langevin sampler provably recovers the sparse signal in polynomial time with near-optimal sample complexity for a broad family of random and deterministic sensing matrices. When the signal is indeed drawn from the postulated prior, we further establish total variation guarantees for posterior sampling after a final denoising step. These results lay a theoretical foundation for statistically and computationally efficient inverse solvers with diffusion priors.

cs.AI / 1 / 2611.23375
Where the Tokens Go: Heat, Entropy and Error in Agentic Coding
Alán Aspuru-Guzik, Varinia Bernales
cs.AI · cond-mat.stat-mech · cs.SE
Abstract
Coding agents are billed by the token, yet software engineering says nothing about what a token actually buys. Here we introduce a theory of software thermodynamics. The theory draws analogues from classical and stochastic thermodynamics, extends them, and applies them to modern agentic coding. We count the tokens an agent generates as its cost and divide that cost into work and heat. The test suite acts as a software Maxwell's daemon that judges every coding change. We test the theory with an analogue of the experiments in which a single molecule is pulled open and let fold again: an agent makes a change to a repository (coding) and then undoes it (uncoding), many times over, and we count the tokens of every model call. The cycle returns the requested edits to where they began, with each direction started from a stored reference tree, and the spread of its cost over repeated cycles defines a software temperature, which rose with the sampling temperature of the model. About 80 per cent of the tokens of a successful run are generated in model calls that leave the requested change where it was, and we call these tokens heat. The free energy of a change, which we estimate by analogy with the equality of Jarzynski, is 14 to 22 per cent of the mean cost of a successful coding run. Coding costs 1.1 to 1.5 times as much as uncoding. The daemon is imperfect: the verdict of a test suite varies with its environment, and a suite that accepts a broken change has a cost in tokens. The practical implication of the proposed theory could be new tools for analysing and optimising coding agents through the lens of thermodynamics.

HardwareDx: A Foundational Graph Model System for Datacenter Machine Repairs
Yuanlin Wen, Elan Markowitz, Zubo Gu, Sami Abu-El-Haija, Bryan Perozzi, Mikhail Galkin, Ali Parviz, Aayush Gupta, Venkata Chivukula, Griffin Hadfield, Aravind Akella, Daniel J. Frame, Vahab Mirrokni, Amin Vahdat

Abstract
The rapid scale-up of AI infrastructure has made datacenter reliability a cornerstone of the cloud business economy. Since hardware failures in hyper-scale AI clusters can stall multi-million dollar training workloads, the downtime of individual machines can cause outsized economic losses. Minimizing machine downtime, therefore, is more important than ever. To address this, we present Hardware Diagnoser (HardwareDx), an AI-driven hardware diagnosis system that applies a graph foundation model approach to automated datacenter maintenance. It allows a single model to diagnose many platforms and accelerate onboarding of new hardware products. Deployed at production scale at Google, HardwareDx yields substantial efficiency gains across diverse compute architectures. Real-world evaluations demonstrate that it reduces production downtime by 18.3% on GPU platforms and 16.1% on TPUs. Furthermore, it significantly accelerates hardware deployment, cutting quality assurance (QA) time by 28.3% for GPUs and 25.1% for TPUs. These results establish HardwareDx as a field-tested solution for maximizing the reliability and cost efficiency of next generation AI fleets.

RFBench: A Simulator-Grounded Multimodal Benchmark for Passive RF Layout Design and Understanding
Jiarui Cui, Boxun Yan
cs.AI · cs.CV · cs.LG
Abstract
While multimodal language models can interpret diagrams and generate structured outputs, their capacity to connect passive radio-frequency (RF) design intent, layout geometry, and electromagnetic behavior remains largely untested. To address this gap, we introduce RFBench, a simulator-grounded dataset and benchmark for passive RF layout design and understanding. The dataset contains 10,000 two-port planar layouts simulated using ADS Momentum, with each layout represented by editable geometric primitives, a raster image, a 16x16 occupancy grid, complex S-parameters at 201 frequency points, a structural category, and an RF response label. Building on these aligned representations, we define seven tasks spanning specification-conditioned layout generation, representation translation, response prediction, simulator-based validation, design diagnosis and improvement, structural understanding, and response classification. Extensive baselines across seven multimodal language models reveal systematic weaknesses in generating structurally valid layouts and predicting electromagnetically faithful responses. We show that RF-specific fine-tuning increases T1a structural validity from 0.0% to 83.2% and the T3 primitive-input within-2-dB rate from 17.7% to 62.8%, demonstrating the value of domain adaptation while leaving considerable room for further progress. RFBench establishes a common testbed for evaluating multimodal RF capabilities and guiding the development of models that connect design intent and layout representations with physical behavior.

cs.AI / 4 / 2611.23445
Why Sub-4-Bit Vision CNNs Collapse and Where Mixed-Precision Recovery Stops
Michael Schroeder
cs.AI · cs.CV · cs.LG
Abstract
Deep vision models operating in resource-constrained environments depend heavily on low-bit quantization, yet compressing weights below 4 bits frequently induces catastrophic accuracy collapse. While mixed-precision recovery strategies aim to rescue accuracy by selectively retaining high-precision parameters, the fundamental mechanics of where and why these models collapse remain poorly understood. In this study, we systematically analyze the anatomy of quantization collapse across standard Vision CNNs (including ResNet and EfficientNet backbones) evaluated on the full 50,000-image ImageNet-1k validation set. First, we map the exact progression of degradation, demonstrating that collapse is highly non-linear and concentrated in late-stage pointwise projections and depthwise layers. Second, we introduce a structured, multi-step recovery waterfall that evaluates selective integer precision (INT4/INT8) and selective floating-point scales. We show that keeping less than 5% of critical layer activations in 8-bit precision recovers up to 92% of the accuracy lost during aggressive sub-4-bit compression. Finally, we bridge the hardware reality gap by evaluating deployment performance on standard ARM and x86 CPU architectures. We show that while low-bit quantization reduces memory storage requirements, standard runtime software bit-unpacking introduces a 1.48x to 21.5x execution slowdown depending on batch size, highlighting a critical trade-off between model footprint and actual edge throughput. Our findings provide a practical blueprint for navigating the limits of sub-4-bit deployment without sacrificing hardware performance.

LusoClin: A Synthetic Clinical Note Dataset for Medical Information Retrieval in European Portuguese

cs.AI · cs.IR
Abstract
Access to large-scale clinical text collections is crucial for advancing medical information retrieval research, including clinical note search, patient cohort identification, and domain-adapted retrieval models. However, real clinical notes are rarely available due to privacy regulations, which particularly limits progress for low-resource languages such as European Portuguese. We present LusoClin, a publicly released dataset of synthetic clinical notes in European Portuguese, created to support privacy-preserving research on clinical text retrieval. LusoClin was generated by pre-processing real clinical data, fine-tuning the open-source Llama 3.2 (3B) instruction-tuned model using Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation, and applying prompt-based clinical note generation. To facilitate semantic indexing and clinical search, the notes are automatically annotated with clinical entities using a BERT-based model. We evaluate LusoClin in terms of utility, fidelity, diversity, and privacy using automatic metrics and human evaluation. Results indicate that the dataset captures clinically relevant language patterns and can support downstream IR applications such as clinical document retrieval and domain-specific model adaptation, although annotators can often distinguish synthetic from real notes and some medical inconsistencies persist.

Abstract
Automatic generation of mathematics assessment items is a growing area in educational artificial intelligence, yet classroom deployment remains challenging. Generated questions must satisfy multiple constraints: mathematical correctness, curriculum alignment, appropriate cognitive difficulty, and educator reviewability. While prior work has advanced text generation, reliable assessment authoring requires granular control over localized examination formats and expert educational judgment. To address this challenge, we present VeriMath, a generalized, human-in-the-loop framework for generating rigorous, curriculum-constrained mathematics assessment drafts. Using annotated reference items, the framework anchors generation to the requested examination section and cognitive reasoning level, then applies sequential automated verification and guided repair before submitting drafts for expert review. We evaluate VeriMath through a national curriculum case study using 4,555 mathematics items from the Vietnamese Grade 12 curriculum and 50 distinct generation requirements covering multiple-choice, true/false, and short-answer formats. Across two model backbones, the framework produces verifier-accepted drafts for 94% (47/50) of requirements per run. Blind expert evaluations confirm high mathematical accuracy and curriculum alignment, with strict teacher-readiness assessments accepting up to 56.8% of generated items. Analysis of rejected drafts reveals persistent domain-agnostic challenges involving formatting, statement validity, and solution-step completeness. These findings demonstrate that VeriMath can bridge generative AI and dependable educational applications by producing highly reviewable assessment drafts within tightly constrained national curriculum frameworks.

cs.AI / 7 / 2611.23476
GUARD: Stabilizing Recursive Self-Improvement with Regret Guidance
Minghe Zhang, Xuetao Kang, Yifei Ming, Yanfei Chen, Han Yu, Yufan Zhuang, Chen-Yu Lee
cs.AI · cs.LG
Abstract
Autonomous AI agents pair a frozen base model with an editable harness of prompts, skills, tool rules, and memory. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) adapts this harness from experience without weight updates, yet self-editing without external graders often backfires: reflection and scalar scores conflate what an edit newly broke with what remains unsolved, causing local regressions, skill forgetting, and memory bloat. We introduce GUARD (Grader-free Unsupervised Environment Design [UED] with Adaptive Rule Distillation), a closed-loop framework for reference-free continual harness evolution. Our key insight is to decompose each task into pre-execution self-checks and guide harness updates via directional regret. Each round grades trajectories against these checks, pinning mastered rules while prioritizing newly broken behaviors, and selects among parallel candidate edits by critic-free group-relative fitness. A Soft-HURT gate then promotes an edit only when gains outweigh regressions, scoping specialized fixes to prevent over-triggering and guaranteeing non-regression on its gated buffer. At test time, one frozen harness runs in a single pass. Across benchmarks on memory, skill evolution, continual task streams, and domain reasoning, GUARD consistently improves performance without catastrophic forgetting or memory pollution while substantially cutting deployment token usage.

cs.AI / 8 / 2611.23508
BOS Summary: The First Token Matters
Hui Zhu, Saleh Zare Zade, Rafi Ibn Sultan, Deng Pan, Arun Ross, Dongxiao Zhu
cs.AI · cs.CL · cs.CV
Abstract
Large vision-language models (LVLMs) and language models (LLMs) often exhibit attention sinks, whereby particular positions, such as the beginning-of-sequence (BOS) token, receive a disproportionate share of attention. Under standard causal masking, however, the BOS query attends only to itself, so the representation that later tokens repeatedly access carries no information about the input. We introduce BOS Summary, a training-free inference-time method that repurposes this persistent pathway to carry input context. At a single transformer layer during prefill, BOS Summary relaxes the causal constraint for the BOS query row alone, letting BOS aggregate all visual and textual input tokens into a self-derived context representation while every other token retains standard causal attention. The enriched representation then remains accessible to the model throughout decoding, with no additional parameters, auxiliary modules, or decoding-time overhead. Across multiple VLM and LLM families and eight multimodal and text-only benchmarks, BOS Summary improves over direct and Chain-of-Thought prompting and outperforms recent sink-intervention methods on multi-step reasoning tasks. A mechanistic analysis shows that making BOS input-specific also weakens its sink dominance and redistributes attention toward content-bearing prompt tokens, indicating that changing what a sink carries reshapes how later layers allocate attention.

Sevda Ebrahimi, Mohammed Saidul Islam, Xiaodan Zhu, Elham Dolatabadi
cs.AI · cs.CL · cs.NE
Abstract
Automated agent design searches for executable architectures that improve LLM-based agent performance, with evolutionary methods using language-model crossover to recombine promising mechanisms for task decomposition, model coordination, and verification. This search, however, is typically guided by aggregate fitness alone, which hides the instance-level successes and failures behind each score. We introduce Execution Guided Genetic Recombination for Agent Design (GRAFT), which uses aggregate fitness for selection and survival and parent-specific execution evidence to guide semantic crossover with integrated mutation. Its feedback harness reuses bounded samples of successful and failed runs from fitness evaluation, withholding reference answers and requiring no additional task executions. We evaluate GRAFT across six reasoning and programming settings using open-weight optimizer and executor models. It achieves a mean test accuracy of 82.0%, exceeding the strongest baseline by 9.8% points. Controlled ablations show that adding execution evidence improves test accuracy with initialization, search rules, repair policies, and evaluation budgets held fixed. Our results support the value of parent-specific execution evidence for evolutionary agent design.

cs.AI · cs.AR
Abstract
Time-series sensing increasingly relies on neural networks, yet deployment on resource-constrained microcontrollers remains challenging. Aggressive model compression can reduce accuracy, while restricting weights to multiplication-free representations introduces further losses. We present BeFit, an end-to-end framework that shifts model capacity from weights to learnable Bernstein polynomial activations. BeFit (i) finds compact Bernstein-activated convolutional neural networks (BeCNNs) through hardware-aware neural architecture search and trains them via knowledge distillation; (ii) projects their weights to multiplication-free codes, freezes the codes, and recovers the resulting accuracy loss through the learnable activations; and (iii) generates model-specific kernels that exploit the projected weights for multiplication-free convolutions. On human activity recognition, BeCNNs are 2.75 percentage points (pp) more accurate on average than ReLU CNNs of identical architecture. On a TI CC3220SF (Cortex-M4), weight projection speeds BeCNNs up by 2.2x on average while losing 0.8 pp, compared with 2.4 pp for ReLU CNNs. Against the MLPerf Tiny DS-CNN reference model running on TensorFlow Lite Micro with CMSIS-NN, the unprojected BeCNN achieves 1.0 pp higher accuracy, 2.2x lower latency, and 6.4x lower flash, while the projected model remains within 1.0 pp of the reference accuracy and runs 5.9x faster. In emulation on a RISC-V core without a hardware multiplier, the instruction-count reduction relative to the DS-CNN increases from 5.2x on the Cortex-M4 to 147x. BeFit also extends to transformers and MLPs, and across all tasks the final models stay within 1.56 pp of their float32 teachers on average.

Abstract
Personality is only weakly and inconsistently signaled by written language, and existing text-based methods typically combine language-model and psycholinguistic representations at the input or decision level. It remains open whether a more deliberate combination of the two views, and a decomposition of the prediction target, can recover more of the signal. We present a three-phase framework for estimating Big Five personality domain scores from life-narrative interview text. It encodes text and psycholinguistic features separately and combines them by concatenation or by a learned weighting, decomposes each domain into contrastively trained facet embeddings instead of predicting the domain directly, and pools the facet embeddings by attention into a domain-level prediction. We compare end-to-end with staged training and ablate the input modalities, their combination, and the facet-pooling strategy. On 1,332 participants from the St. Louis Personality and Aging Network (SPAN) study, facet embeddings reach AUC up to 0.740, and domain-level R2 reaches 0.328, highest for Openness. End-to-end training gives lower error than staged training in every domain, and attention pooling gives the lowest error in every domain. Combining the two views lowers error relative to text alone for Conscientiousness and Agreeableness, whereas a learned weighting of the views shows no consistent advantage over concatenation. The framework provides facet- level predictions that a domain-only model cannot, and it improves modestly on a regression from the raw features in four of the five domains.

Abstract
When LLM agents pass intermediate judgments downstream without uncertainty, later decisions may treat tentative assumptions as facts. Effective uncertainty propagation must preserve information for correction and update inherited beliefs as new evidence arrives. Yet scalar scores omit information needed for revision, while detailed descriptions and reflection incur additional costs. We introduce Latent Uncertainty, a latent-space estimator that preserves uncertainty-relevant information without lengthy descriptions. Building on this, we propose LProp (Latent Uncertainty Propagation), which revises inherited answer distributions using latent representations and new evidence without additional trajectory sampling. We evaluate both methods across multiple-choice, yes/no, open-ended question answering, and mathematical reasoning tasks. Our approach outperforms baselines on most metrics, while LProp achieves the lowest mean inference-token usage in all eight propagation settings. Matched feature ablations further demonstrate that inherited latent content improves error recovery beyond answer probabilities or model capacity alone.
