Dissecting an Unexplored SASS Control-Code Field: Barrier Exemption and Programmable Warp Priority
Ziwen Wang, Qi Luo, Kunlin Li, Changxi Liu, Dongsheng Wang, Yun Chen
cs.AR · cs.DC · cs.PF
Abstract
Every instruction in NVIDIA's native GPU ISA (SASS) carries a control code that guides hardware scheduling, and prior work has decoded its known fields to optimize GPU kernels. However, one control-code field remains unexplored: it appears over 500000 times in NVIDIA's closed-source libraries such as cuBLAS and cuDNN, yet nvcc never emits it when compiling user programs. This paper presents the first systematic study of this control-code field across GPU architectures from Volta to Blackwell. Using instruction-level microbenchmarks, we show that the field controls two independent hardware mechanisms: barrier exemption (EXEMPT), which allows instructions blocked by a pending barrier to issue early during the barrier wait, and programmable warp priority (START, TILE, and END), which moves warps across three priority levels in the hardware scheduler. We identify the conditions under which each mechanism improves GPU kernel performance and implement a post-compilation binary optimizer that places these marks directly in compiled binaries without modifying source code or the compiler. Evaluated across six GPUs spanning four architectures, our optimizations speed up representative kernels by up to 31.9%, and the optimizer accelerates production kernels in llama.cpp and vLLM by up to 5.4% and end-to-end LLM inference by up to 3.6%.

TechReport: Implementing CHERI in gem5
Philipp Schmitz, Vishwas Vasuki Gautam, Tobias Jauch, Anna Lena Duque Antón, Johannes Müller, Dominik Stoffel, Wolfgang Kunz
cs.AR
Abstract
Despite countless mitigation efforts, memory safety issues still prevail. The recently discovered security issues in PHP underline this fact. One of the most promising approaches to solving this problem is the concept of Capability Hardware Enhanced RISC Instructions (CHERI). There is a well-developed ecosystem of ISA simulators, compilers, operating systems, and hardware designs that support CHERI. However, the lack of a simulator modeling microarchitectural detail hinders efficient and fast design space exploration for CHERI-enhanced designs means the performance impact of CHERI remains understudied. Therefore, we present gem5-CHERI: a CHERI-enhanced adaptation of the gem5 simulator that can boot the CheriBSD operating system and run custom workloads. The simulator is available open-source on GitHub.

Reliable arithmetic circuits using less reliable (sub-digital) logic
Trevor McCourt, Ila R. Fiete, Neil Gershenfeld, Isaac L. Chuang
cs.AR · cond-mat.stat-mech · physics.app-ph
Abstract
The frequent static failure of CMOS logic gates at ultra-low voltages has historically been perceived as a strict barrier to extreme voltage scaling: this paper introduces a statistical circuit law proving this intuition wrong. We discovered a universal power law connecting gate and circuit static failure probabilities, revealing that circuit failure requires the simultaneous breakdown of an entire gate cluster rather than a single component. Because the required cluster size increases rapidly as voltage drops, low-voltage \textit{sub-digital} logic exhibits surprising inherent resilience to static failure. This insight stems from new theoretical tools we developed to quantify static failure, extending well beyond conventional voltage-margin analysis. Consequently, sub-digital processors could potentially offer a viable, near-term solution to drastically reduce the energy demands of AI.

Hypnos: A Dual-Phase End-to-End Platform for Scalable Continual Learning at the Edge
Guilherme Guedes, Marco Apolinario Lainez, Charlotte Frenkel
cs.AR · cs.AI · cs.CV
Abstract
Continual learning (CL) enables neural networks to adapt to non-stationary data streams by mitigating catastrophic forgetting, offering a path to robust, private, and adaptable edge devices. Yet, porting CL to real-world edge devices remains challenging for two reasons: (i) online operation, where sensor data arrives one sample at a time and the device must adapt on-the-fly, and (ii) the low footprint of edge devices, which makes traditional error backpropagation training prohibitive. Inspired by the brain's wake and sleep cycles, the former for rapid adaptation with minimal resources and the latter for long-term consolidation, we introduce Hypnos, an open-source dual-phase platform for efficient CL at the edge. In the wake phase (e.g., daily operation), Hypnos relies on a low-footprint system-on-chip with a RISC-V microcontroller unit (MCU) targeting efficient inference and supporting lightweight gradient-free prototype updates. In the sleep phase (e.g., night-time charging), where wall-plug energy and larger memory budgets are available, a smart charger performs rehearsal-based gradient updates for consolidation. Deployed on a ZCU104 field-programmable gate array (FPGA) and synthesized in a 28-nm process, Hypnos is benchmarked on the CORe50 NICv2-391 protocol. It sets a new state-of-the-art accuracy of 78.6%-81.6% for edge CL systems, with an on-device latency of 7.79s-10.54s per sample depending on activation precision, and requires $3.8\times$ fewer learning steps and $22\times$ less learning compute than quantized latent replay at higher accuracy and comparable latency.

Mechanistic Critics for Sample-Efficient NPU Design-Space Exploration
Yicheng He, Yuqi Xue, Tianyang Wu, Jian Huang, Bin Hu
cs.AR
Abstract
NPU design-space exploration for LLM inference mainly relies on an expensive simulator that often returns only scalar feedback such as latency and power. Such feedback can rank evaluated configurations, but gives little information for deciding why a configuration is slow or which architecture parameter should be changed next. This limitation is especially severe because prefill and decode workloads can be limited by different resources, including compute throughput and HBM bandwidth. We propose CriticNPU, a sample-efficient DSE framework built around an online-calibrated mechanistic critic for NPU architecture design. The critic uses explicit hardware limits to evaluate NPU configurations: before simulation, it estimates whether a proposed configuration is likely to improve over the current best and filters weak candidates; after simulation, it aggregates operator-level runtimes into prefill/decode bottleneck summaries and predicts the effect of candidate parameter changes. We instantiate the critic with a Roofline-style model that derives compute and memory limits from architecture parameters and calibrates per-operator-type effective limits using simulator observations. And CriticNPU combines this critic with a workload extractor and an architecture planner to propose configurations. Across six LLM workloads and 16 deployment configurations per model, CriticNPU achieves best-or-tied-best latency in 74% of prefill and 87.5% of decode settings while using roughly half the simulator calls of competitive DSE baselines. We conduct extensive ablation studies and detailed analyses to validate the effectiveness of our method from multiple perspectives. Our code is available at https://github.com/bruno686/CriticNPU.

MicroAssert: Microarchitecture-Aware Structured Assertion Generation for CPU Verification
Hongqin Lyu, Yonghao Wang, Zhiteng Chao, Wenxing Li, Tiancheng Wang, Evangeline F. Y. Young, Huawei Li
cs.AR · cs.SE
Abstract
Automatic assertion generation reduces manual verification effort, yet existing approaches struggle to capture microarchitectural behaviors and cross-region interactions in CPUs. We present MicroAssert, a microarchitecture-aware framework that identifies functional regions directly from RTL and generates local and composite assertions through structured contracts and deterministic verification primitives. Coverage-guided feedback further improves verification completeness by progressively expanding proof-relevant RTL coverage. Evaluated on five open-source RISC-V CPUs against three existing assertion generation approaches, MicroAssert achieves 100% syntax correctness and complete branch, statement, and toggle coverage, with an average proven rate of 74.82% and Proof Core coverage of 90.96%. Mutation testing further demonstrates its advantage, achieving an average error detection rate of 28.73%, 1.99 to 3.51 times higher than existing methods. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of microarchitecture-aware assertion generation.

cs.AR / 12 / 2611.24458
A Runtime System for Mitigating Crossbar Port Contention on SM-Partitioned GPUs
Ziwen Wang, Qi Luo, Kunlin Li, Changxi Liu, Dongsheng Wang, Yun Chen
cs.DC · cs.AR
Abstract
To avoid scheduling delays when running concurrent workloads on a GPU, Streaming Multiprocessor (SM) partitioning mechanisms such as CUDA Green Contexts restrict each workload to separate SMs. Despite this partitioning, concurrent workloads still significantly slow down latency-critical workloads, which recent studies attribute to shared L2 cache and memory contention. However, contention also occurs at the crossbar ports connecting each Graphics Processing Cluster (GPC) of SMs to the L2 cache, as all SMs in a GPC share one port. Green Contexts spread workloads across GPCs, placing concurrent workloads in the same GPCs and forcing latency-critical memory requests to queue behind background requests. Packing workloads into separate GPCs avoids this contention, but forces latency-critical memory requests through fewer ports, limiting memory bandwidth. Consequently, neither spreading nor packing is always faster across workloads and GPUs. Based on these observations, we present GPCPlace, a runtime system that dynamically selects between spreading and packing by profiling workloads on the target GPU to estimate both slowdowns, and hooks kernel launches in the CUDA driver to set SM masks without application modifications. Across 14 GPUs and 112 workload cases, GPCPlace speeds up latency-critical workloads by up to 1.15x on average and 2.38x maximum over Green Contexts without degrading throughput.

Compute Before You Digitize: ADC-less Mixed-Signal Processing for Scalable Cryogenic Qubit Readout
Qirui Zhang, Ben Toby, He Wang, Benjamin Lienhard, David Blaauw, Dennis Sylvester
quant-ph · cs.AR · cs.ET · eess.SP
Abstract
We introduce DIRAC, an ADC-less in-cryostat qubit readout architecture that uses analog computing to redraw the analog-digital boundary. Directly operating on the front-end's analog output, passive complex mixers perform the equivalent of digital demodulation, ping-pong active-RC integrators average their outputs into down-sampled per-qubit traces, and a time-domain stage digitizes them, eliminating Nyquist-rate ADCs. A TX-RX co-design derives the mixers' local oscillators from the readout transmitter's baseband rather than per-tone PLLs. A per-line calibration flow trains the matched filter jointly with the neural network, improving fidelity and enabling low-bit-width, low-voltage digital processing. Designed in 22 nm FD-SOI and evaluated at 4 K on 1.12M experimental shots, DIRAC matches the fidelity of a floating-point (FP32) digital pipeline for readout windows down to 750 ns, at 31.6$\times$ and 238$\times$ lower energy than the fixed-point (FxP) and FP32 pipelines. It cuts the total 4 K power per physical qubit by 50.4% and 68.6% relative to FxP and room-temperature flex cables, respectively. At a fixed logical-qubit count and 4 K budget, this yields, against FxP, a code distance larger by 2 to 6 and a 1.6-7.3$\times$ (Willow) and 4.9-204$\times$ (SI1000, $p = 10^{-3}$) lower logical error rate.

cs.CR / 1 / 2611.23507
ACaM: Automated Capability Modeling for Agentic AI Security
Monika Santra, Dhilung Kirat, Qiushi Wu, Kevin Eykholt, Xiaokui Shu, Ian Molloy
cs.CR
Abstract
In agentic AI systems, an LLM invokes tools that hold standing access to credentials, private data, filesystems, and external services. Such agents are increasingly deployed without an answer to a basic question: what can an agent access, exfiltrate, and propagate, independent of what it is designed for or is observed to do? The question goes unanswered because existing approaches trust a tool's natural-language description as a proxy for its behavior. But nothing enforces that the description and its implementation agree. This gap is known as Description-Code Inconsistency (DCI). DCI enables a threat class called capability laundering, in which a tool's implementation contains dangerous behavior that its description omits. The behavior may come from incidental drift or a supply-chain compromise. It runs silently whenever an LLM invokes the tool for its stated, benign purpose. We present ACaM, a neurosymbolic approach to capability modeling that derives each tool's capabilities from its code, so a laundered capability cannot hide behind a benign description. In ACaM, static analysis grounds an LLM in code-derived facts, and no LLM output can override a fact that static analysis has established. The LLM supplies only the behavioral meaning that those facts cannot express. ACaM compiles agent source code into the Agent Capability Property Graph (ACPG) and uses it to reconstruct threat chains that span multiple tool calls. We evaluate ACaM on 43 real-world agents, including 9 multi-agent systems. On 24 manually annotated agents, it recovers capability properties with 98.3% macro-F1 and reconstructs injected threat chains with a score of 0.980, 8 points above the strongest baseline. Applied to all 43 unmodified agents, it discovers hundreds of structural vulnerabilities, ten of which we confirm with proof-of-concept exploits.

A-Tag: Cryptographic File Tagging with Enforced Live Human Presence
Mohammed Gharib, Sam Burns, Martin Zizi
cs.CR
Abstract
The increasing autonomy of software agents and the proliferation of AI-generated content have weakened the reliability of digital actions as evidence of human involvement. Existing mechanisms, such as digital signatures and authentication protocols, verify identity and integrity, but do not establish whether a live human was present at the time an action was performed. In this paper, we introduce A-Tag, a system for verifiable human-in-the-loop tagging of digital artifacts. A-Tag cryptographically binds a file to a verified instance of live human presence at the moment of tagging. The resulting tag serves as a persistent and transferable proof that the action was triggered by a live human, without making claims about the origin, identity of the actor, or semantic content of the file. A-Tag is a modular framework combining liveness verification based on micro-motion signals shaped by human motor control, a secure cryptographic binding between the verified event and the artifact, and a publicly verifiable logging mechanism enabling independent validation. We formalize security properties of human presence signals, define an adversarial model capturing automated and relay attacks, and analyze the system's guarantees and limitations. We implement A-Tag on commodity devices and evaluate it under realistic conditions. Our evaluation shows that A-Tag provides cryptographically sound artifact binding with deterministic verification, while enabling robust recovery under real-world transformations, achieving over 99 percent success for image-based artifacts, and maintaining sub-second verification and practical tagging latency.

cs.CR / 3 / 2611.23660
Protecting Web Applications using a Multimodal AI-based System for Classifying Web Injection Attacks
Rodrigo Branco, Vinicius Cogo, Ibéria Medeiros
cs.CR
Abstract
Web applications have been essential to accessing and managing online services. Made available with weaknesses, much due to their rapid development and human error, they are exposed to frequent web injection attacks, leaving security analysts overwhelmed with threats and alerts that often lack critical details for proper risk assessment. Detecting these attacks requires inspecting the payload of network traffic packets, which becomes inaccessible when traffic is encrypted via HTTPS, as encryption hides the content of the traffic. This paper introduces a Multimodal Artificial Intelligence (AI) system to protect online services that rely on web application security by detecting and classifying web injection attacks, and provides security analysts with information to support attack prevention and incident response. The system employs unsupervised Machine Learning (ML) to flag potentially anomalous Network Flows (NetFlows). The corresponding data recorded in Web Server Logs (WebLogs) is then analysed using a heuristic framework based on Natural Language Processing (NLP) and supervised ML to detect and classify web injection attacks. Finally, the resulting classifications are scrutinised using a Similarity Search Engine (SSE) based on Locality Sensitive Hashing (LSH) to validate them. The solution handles encrypted traffic by analysing NetFlows and WebLogs, the latter in their natural, unencrypted form, by leveraging NetFlow-level metadata for anomaly detection and analysing web server logs after TLS termination, thereby avoiding any additional in-network traffic decryption. It was evaluated in the classification of eight web injection attack classes. The results demonstrated its ability to accurately identify attacks and their classes, achieving an F_1 score of 91% and an accuracy of 95%, and offering valuable insights for alert prioritisation.

cs.CR / 4 / 2611.23669
FlowSH: Detecting Web Attacks by Correlating Anomalous Network Flows and Endpoint Logs
Nuno Durão, Rodrigo Branco, Vinicius V. Cogo, Ibéria Medeiros
cs.CR
Abstract
Web applications compose the core of internet services, rendering them prominent targets for audacious attackers. Among web attacks, SQL injection (SQLi) remains a persistent, damaging web applications connected to databases. The widespread adoption of HTTPS has been a critical advancement for online security, ensuring the confidentiality and integrity of communications by encrypting network payloads. However, it also renders traditional Network Intrusion Detection Systems (NIDS) less effective, as these typically rely on packet inspection of plaintext traffic. To access encrypted payloads, some NIDS resort to TLS-interception proxies, which leads to data leaks and security risks. This paper presents FlowSH, a system for detecting web attacks that is agnostic to whether the traffic is encrypted (HTTPS) or not (HTTP). Rather than decrypting packets in transit, FlowSH correlates flow-level metadata (NetFlows) with endpoint logs, which inherently contain decrypted payloads after reaching the web server. The system combines unsupervised machine learning to flag anomalous NetFlows and similarity search over server-side logs using Locality Sensitive Hashing (LSH) to confirm attacks. We implemented and evaluated FlowSH in a testbed with multiple web scanners and demonstrated its detection effectiveness, detecting 70% of SQLi attacks missed by ModSecurity, a leading web application firewall.

Data Poisoning Attacks to Locally Differentially Private Triangle Counting Protocols
Tingxuan Han, Wei Tong, Zijian Wang, Sheng Zhong
cs.CR
Abstract
Local differential privacy (LDP) has become a crucial paradigm for privacy-preserving graph analytics, enabling graph analytics tasks such as subgraph counting without requiring a trusted curator. However, while LDP provides strong privacy guarantees, the integrity and robustness of LDP subgraph counting protocols in the presence of malicious participants remain poorly understood. In particular, since data are randomized locally before collection, it is inherently difficult to distinguish malicious users from honest ones based solely on their submitted reports, and small, protocol-compliant local manipulations can be systematically amplified through reconstruction and calibration into large global estimation bias. In this paper, we use LDP triangle counting as a representative task to characterize the vulnerability of LDP subgraph counting to data poisoning attacks. For both non-interactive and interactive LDP triangle counting protocols, we analyze their attack surfaces and develop a unified gain-driven framework that captures how adversarial users can manipulate calibrated subgraph count estimates, which we instantiate on representative protocols of both types. Extensive experiments on four real-world graph datasets demonstrate that these attacks can significantly distort triangle count estimates across different protocols and adversarial settings. Moreover, we show that existing and straightforward defenses are insufficient to mitigate these attacks, underscoring the need for robustness mechanisms tailored to LDP subgraph counting.

JITAtlas: Checking Lifetime and Protection Obligations in Compiler Rewrites
Baihong Chen, Wen Li
cs.CR · cs.SE
Abstract
Compiler rewrites can preserve returned values while violating object lifetime or ownership. Such failures arise when a rewrite changes when an object remains live, whether a borrowed pointer stays supported, or what ownership reaches the caller. We present JITAtlas, a source-level checker that reconstructs reference and target computations from optimizer code and checks valid uses, continuous borrow support, and caller-visible ownership. On a 58-input benchmark constructed and labeled independently of JITAtlas output, JITAtlas detects all 29 defects and reports none of 29 safe inputs; PyRefcon detects 20 defects and CpyChecker 18. Across three CPython snapshots, JITAtlas extracts 3,332 rewrite alternatives, retains 801 under recovered receiving contexts, and reports 194 violations. Manual review confirms 92 reports, giving 47.42% precision. End-to-end analysis takes 35.56-42.31 s per snapshot. JITAtlas further identifies 15 new bugs across five failure classes, each with a reproducible proof of concept.

Expressiveness and Convertibility of Rule-Based Access Control Policies
Amir Masoumzadeh, Paliath Narendran, Padmavathi Iyer
cs.CR
Abstract
Rule-based access control models such as attribute-based access control support flexible policies based on rules with conditional expressions. The design choices in those models such as what is allowed in the conditional expressions or supporting deny rules may impact the range of the policies that are expressible. In this paper, we propose a systematic approach to investigate the semantics and compare the expressiveness of various rule-based access control models that can be built based on different design choices of rule structure and rule composition. Furthermore, we investigate the problem of convertibility of a policy from one rule-based model to another. This question is critical for policy migration to ensure that a given policy instance in a source model is expressible in a target model. Some of our major results in this paper include well-formedness properties for policy semantics, expressiveness hierarchy of models, and computational complexity of policy convertibility, all having important implications on the design and application of rule-based access control policy models.

Authenticating IoT Data on Ethereum after Pectra and Fusaka: A Cost Study of Signature Schemes, Batching and Anchoring for Agricultural Supply Chain Finance
Ming-Fong Sie, Jian-Hong Chen, Gwan-yen Lin, Yen-Shuo Chen, Shih-wei Liao
cs.CR · cs.DC
Abstract
Blockchain-based supply chain finance can turn the sensor-recorded production history of smallholder farms into verifiable credit evidence, but only if every record is authenticated and anchored at a cost that scales to large device fleets. Ethereum's 2025 Pectra and Fusaka upgrades changed this cost landscape: they added precompiles for BLS12-381 and P-256, repriced calldata and MODEXP, and capped transaction gas at $2^{24}$. We organize the authentication and anchoring of IoT records into three trust levels, from posting a Merkle root through a trusted aggregator to verifying every device signature on-chain, and implement four replay-protected signature designs: ECDSA over secp256k1 and P-256, BLS aggregate signatures with on-chain hash-to-curve, and a pseudonymous identity-based signature with batch verification. Measured as signed transactions under the rules before and after both upgrades, the upgrades mainly changed which designs are feasible, not their cost. Batching and Merkle anchoring cut the cost of ECDSA authentication sixfold, to 8,963 gas per record, and secp256k1 ECDSA remains the cheapest authenticated design: P-256 costs 1.6 times as much, the identity-based design 2.7 times and BLS aggregation 3.9 times, dominated by on-chain hashing to the curve. One transaction carries at most 1,754 ECDSA-authenticated records but only 411 BLS-aggregated ones. On a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W, pairing-based signing takes 5.7 ms against 0.29 ms for ECDSA. Pairing-based designs pay off only when the application needs their additional properties, and the identity-based design adds key escrow at the key generation centre. The benchmark harness is released for reproducibility.

Abdulaziz Abdulghaffar, Ashraf Matrawy
cs.CR · cs.NI
Abstract
As cellular networks transition toward 5G-Advanced and Sixth Generation (6G) architectures, Network Slicing (NS) remains essential for multiplexing heterogeneous services over shared physical infrastructure. However, deploying critical Ultra-Reliable Low Latency Communications (URLLC) alongside standard broadband introduces severe cross-slice vulnerabilities. The implicit assumption that logical slicing inherently guarantees security fails against data plane exploits, as shared User Plane Functions (UPFs) remain susceptible to resource starvation and protocol tunneling. To address this, we propose the Slice Isolation-as-a-Service framework, which treats topological data plane isolation as an on-demand, monetizable capability. We formulate the multi-UPF resource allocation problem as a Mixed-Integer Nonlinear Programming (MINLP) model to strictly enforce physical and virtual isolation boundaries based on tenant security tiers, minimizing provisioning costs and end-to-end latency. To validate the framework, we engineered a novel containerized Fifth Generation (5G) testbed integrating Free5GC with Nokia Containerlab. It also rejects an intact device whose policy left the image writable, a verdict no integrity check can reach. Attention blocking suggests why: a text command acts through its own positions, whereas visual encoding spreads an image command and its target across the instruction page. Abstract
Keyword Private Information Retrieval (Keyword PIR) allows users to retrieve data associated with specific keywords from a database while protecting query privacy. However, existing Keyword PIR schemes supporting boolean retrieval either incur high computational overhead due to multiple database traversals, or fail to support universal boolean computation. We propose PMKPIR, a novel keyword PIR scheme supporting both parallel multi-keyword queries and universal boolean computation. We utilize the single instruction multiple data (SIMD) capability of BFV homomorphic encryption to propose an interleaved batching method, and design IBPIR based on this method, achieving the private matching of multiple keywords in a single database traversal. Furthermore, we design a boolean query processing method, extending the parallel capability of interleaved batching from keyword querying to boolean query computation, to support universal boolean computation and accelerate boolean operations. Building upon IBPIR, we integrate this method to further design PMKPIR. To the best of our knowledge, PMKPIR is the first Keyword PIR scheme to support multi-keyword batch matching within boolean queries. Security analysis demonstrates that, consistent with existing PIR schemes supporting boolean retrieval, PMKPIR preserves the core security guarantees of classic PIR. Compared with state-of-the-art schemes, PMKPIR reduces query time, communication overhead, storage overhead, and peak memory by up to 79.06%, 75.00%, 97.92%, and 80.26%, respectively.

Abstract
LLM serving systems store, offload, and share KV caches, exposing token-level representations to infrastructure operators and co-tenants. Shuffled obfuscation combines secret linear transforms with fresh permutations, claiming security from b! possible shufflings. We show that input symmetry invalidates this counting argument: security depends on distinguishable outputs under chosen inputs. Repeated tokens produce identical first-layer Value rows, making every row permutation leave the data unchanged. Only auxiliary structures such as a single-row recovery marker vary, reducing the effective state space from b! to b. We construct Repeat-to-Reveal. The attacker collects the b distinguishable states from its own probes and exploits their rank-one differences to recover an equivalent denoiser without knowing the defender's secret parameters. A one-time calibration transfers across requests sharing the same secret epoch, enabling passive token-multiset recovery from subsequently observed cache blocks through public-model dictionary matching. We instantiate the attack on official KV-Cloak and evaluate 3,000 real WildChat user prompts across nine models and eleven configurations. The attack recovers the secret parameters with high accuracy and achieves 100 percent token-multiset recovery on GPU. Refreshing row-level secrets between epochs interrupts cross-request transfer, confirming secret reuse scope as the operative vulnerability. We further confirm orbit collapse on two other open-source defenses: the sequence-permutation implementation of Thomas et al. and PermLLM. The KV-Cloak developers invited a detailed report through their private vulnerability reporting channel.

cs.CR · cs.AI · cs.LG
Abstract
Prompt injection is the dominant unsolved security risk for LLM agents, and the community now agrees that robustness must be measured against adaptive attackers rather than fixed benchmark injections. Many adaptive red teamers exist, and most are built to maximize attack success rate (ASR). Yet ASR counts how often a target breaks, not in how many different ways. A red teamer can achieve a high ASR by reusing a few techniques that work, leaving the others untested and absent from the attacks used to harden models. We present AutoPI, an adaptive red teamer designed to find many different ways to break a target, not just to break it often. AutoPI uses PIAtlas, a taxonomy of prompt-injection techniques, both to guide its search and to measure coverage. For each scenario, an attacker LLM writes an injection for every sub-technique in the taxonomy and then reworks the ones that fail using feedback from an LLM judge. The method is black-box and training-free, it plugs into existing benchmarks in place of their fixed attack templates, and it stays up to date as the taxonomy evolves. We evaluate AutoPI on AgentDojo and IPI Arena against open-weight and proprietary target models. Alongside ASR, we report technique coverage, the fraction of taxonomy classes, techniques, and sub-techniques that yield at least one successful injection. On AgentDojo, AutoPI finds a successful injection against Qwen3.6-35B in all six classes of the taxonomy and for more than 90% of its techniques. Against Claude Haiku 5.5, the most robust target we evaluate, it achieves between 20% and 50% higher ASR and between 25% and 400% higher class-level coverage than recent state-of-the-art adaptive red teamers, while requiring no training. We release our code and the generated attacks to support reproducible, coverage-aware evaluation.

Forensic investigators must decide which suspicious files to examine first. Abstract
Function-level vulnerability detectors often exhibit fix reversal, assigning a higher vulnerability probability to a fixed version than to its vulnerable counterpart. Fixes usually lengthen functions, and larger length increases are associated with more severe reversal. Code-transformation experiments indicate that fix reversal mainly stems from a length shortcut: vulnerability probability increases with function length when content is fixed. We propose CFVul to address this problem. Sliding-window encoding covers complete functions, retaining fix information beyond the truncation boundary. During training, a content constraint encourages the vulnerable version to receive a higher vulnerability probability under a common length input. During inference, a length constraint averages vulnerability probabilities over fixed reference lengths, reducing the influence of actual length changes. On PrimeVul, CFVul achieves a fix-pair ranking metric, PairRank, of 59.4\%, exceeding the existing methods compared. For fixes that increase function length by more than 15\%, PairRank rises from CodeBERT's 25.8\% to 48.4\%. PairRank also improves in experiments with four additional models and three additional datasets. By weakening the length shortcut, CFVul reduces cases in which fixed versions receive higher vulnerability probabilities than vulnerable versions. It requires only existing fix pairs and applies to multiple pretrained code models, facilitating adoption in existing detectors.

cs.CR · cs.AI · cs.SE
Abstract
Frontier coding agents increasingly exhibit overeagerness, taking surprising, sometimes reckless actions beyond a user's mandate --- reported in recent system cards from frontier model developers. These cases are surfaced through internal deployment monitoring, which requires private traffic and is out of reach for open-weight models and independent evaluators. Automated alignment audits are the natural alternative, but capable models increasingly recognise the synthetic setup and adjust their behaviour. We introduce Continuation Audits, a pipeline that grounds the auditor on a prefix drawn from a real coding-agent transcript and directs it to continue the trajectory toward a seeded behaviour. Because the prefix is drawn from a real session, the auditor only needs to maintain a realistic setting rather than manufacturing it. We validate the method on SWE-Chat prefixes: on a paired subset of 90 audits a judge cannot reliably distinguish continuations from their source sessions (realism win rate 0.42 vs.\ 0.43), and across all 900 audits verbalized eval-awareness does not exceed the rate observed in the unaudited real sessions. Applying the pipeline to three recent models across three seeds, we find each model leads a different seed --- DeepSeek~V4~Pro on colleague-credentials misuse, GPT-5.6~Terra on file-permission bypasses, and Kimi~K3 on treating diagnostic questions as instructions. Kimi~K3 additionally continues to bypass file-permission protections after an explicit CLAUDE.md prohibition while the other two stop entirely, corroborating Moonshot's own report of excessive proactiveness.

cs.CR / 22 / 2611.24586
Playing the SMR Game with Existential Honesty
Zeta Avarikioti, Odysseas Sofikitis, Christos Stefo
cs.CR
Abstract
State machine replication protocols are usually proven secure in the honest-Byzantine setting, which requires an honest supermajority of validators. Deployed systems offer no such guarantee: validators participate for profit and may deviate from the protocol whenever doing so increases their gains. In our work, every validator is rational or Byzantine, and none is honest. Rational validators may collude with each other and with the Byzantine ones, who may also bribe them to deviate. Known impossibility results show that, without honest validators, clients that decide whether to accept a transaction based on a non-interactive certificate and without further communication cannot be kept safe. To bypass these results, we let clients relay the certificates they receive to full nodes and wait before confirming transactions. We also assume that one full node, whose identity is unknown, is honest and always online. Under this assumption, we build a finalization layer over any certifiable quorum-based protocol in a synchronous network. Clients run an existing freezing gadget and fetch past certificates from the honest full node, which makes the protocol \emph{always-safe}: no two honest clients confirm conflicting ledgers, for any strategy of the validators. We incentivize participation through rewards, which the adversary may use to bribe rational validators into censoring transactions. In this setting, we formalize censorship and characterize it tightly: paying only with his rewards, the adversary censors less than a $\bw$ fraction of the available fees at each height, where $\bw$ is the fraction of the quorum he signs, and every coin of censorship beyond that comes from his own funds.

Abstract
Local differential privacy (LDP) is vulnerable to output manipulation by malicious clients. Zero-knowledge proofs can enforce correct report computation, but clients may still selectively drop out after inspecting their outputs. Prior work combines zero-knowledge proofs with homomorphic encryption to hide reports from clients and prevent selective dropout, but incurs substantial computational cost. We instead develop a three-message lightweight verification framework for robust histogram estimation that uses proofs of plaintext evaluation to restrict output manipulation to selective dropout. Across the evaluated settings for PI-RAPPOR and Hadamard Response, mean per-client online latency remains below 500 milliseconds. We further establish tight error bounds showing that, for RAPPOR, PI-RAPPOR, and Hadamard Response, restricting malicious clients to selective dropout reduces attack-dependent error by a factor proportional to the square root of the domain size compared with output manipulation. Additionally, when client protocols cannot be modified, we propose server-side consistency checks for RAPPOR and Hadamard Response. These checks improve robustness without client-side cryptography and can be applied post-hoc to collected reports, offering an alternative under different deployment constraints. Experiments demonstrate that both verification and consistency checks substantially reduce attack error for certain mechanisms, with consistency checks yielding errors intermediate between those obtained with verification and those under unrestricted output manipulation.

Abstract
Stablecoins can move value continuously across programmable networks, and Web3 wallets can authorize those transfers with cryptographic signatures, but neither capability, standing alone, establishes a complete commercial transaction. A blockchain may prove that a transaction satisfied protocol rules, and a wallet may prove that sufficient signing authority existed; neither proves who initiated the transaction, for which legal entity, under what current authority, against which current compliance evidence, on what exact instruction, or with what settlement and accounting outcome. We describe the ChainIT Transaction Truth Architecture, a zero-trust control, execution, and evidence architecture that places verified individual and organizational identity, the organizational authority record and authority policy of the ChainIT Authority Protocol, transaction-specific runtime compliance decisions, exact-digest approval, atomic capacity reservation, and a single-use Execution Authorization Credential in front of wallet execution, and that records settlement, reconciliation, and lifecycle evidence after the transaction. The architecture separates five boundaries: control of a key is not identity, identity is not organizational authority, authority is not compliance, compliance is not execution authority, and network confirmation is not complete commercial settlement. We describe wallet and custody profiles, including a multi-party computation (MPC) profile in which custody security is kept independent of business authority, stablecoin and Web3 evidence domains, layered finality, the U.S. stablecoin regulatory context as of September 2026, and a phased deployment in which pilot success requires that the control invariants hold under attack and failure.

Abstract
AI-driven attacks learn the models of cyber-physical systems (CPS) by passively observing controller and plant signals, then use this knowledge to act covertly. This work applies Adversarial Machine Learning as a defense, injecting small perturbations into the measurements the attacker observes to degrade an artificial neural network (ANN)-based system identification (SI) attack. The perturbations are derived from input gradients of several independently trained identification models, aggregated into a generalized perturbation, and confined to the transient regimes that carry most of the dynamic information. A sparsity parameter further restricts them to the most influential samples, with negligible cost in effectiveness. On a simulated DC motor networked control system, the proposed perturbations induce larger prediction errors than stochastic poisoning of equal root-mean-square magnitude, and the advantage widens as the magnitude grows. This limits the defense's operating range, which is intended for decoy environments such as CPS honeynets. Additional results indicate that the designed poisoning signals can also degrade N4SID-based system identification, providing evidence of their transferability beyond the ANN-based models originally targeted.

The same command can require opposite safety decisions in different states, so an incorrect answer may reflect missing information rather than poor reasoning. We propose an answerability audit: does the model receive the information needed to decide? The audit records the model's inputs and pairs the same command with two states requiring opposite answers. The paired score counts a pair only when both answers are correct. We add rules, then state values, to the model's input. In an author-built test of 15 pairs from three systems with four language models, none reliably distinguished the paired cases without state, even with rules. With state, scores ranged from 0 to 13 correct pairs out of 15; three models improved. With text alone, one model always allowed commands and another always denied them. Their overall (raw) accuracies differed by 32 percentage points; both scored 50% balanced accuracy, which weights safe and unsafe cases equally, and no correct pairs. A rule evaluator matched all 15 pairs by applying the same rules that supplied the expected answers; this is not an independent safety test. The audit complements systems that check actions against safety rules: it checks whether the model receives the information needed for those decisions. Abstract
Vision Transformers (ViTs) now underpin the visual encoders of most multimodal models, but this success comes at a cost: relying on third-party pretrained checkpoints leaves these systems open to backdoor attacks. Existing test-time detection methods rely on either the predicted label or intermediate embeddings, limiting their applicability across diverse tasks and incurring substantial computational overhead. In this work, we study how backdoor triggers affect the multi-head attention mechanism of ViTs and identify two distinct anomalous patterns: $\textit{complete attention hijacking}$, causing the attention to exhibit abnormally high inter-head spatial overlap, and $\textit{partial attention hijacking}$, causing an abnormally large variance in the concentration of the attention distribution. DetectViT quantifies the two hijacking phenomena via an inter-head consistency score and an inter-head entropy variance score, with thresholds estimated from a small out-of-distribution (OOD) calibration set drawn from an arbitrary source. Across four representative attacks, diverse architectures (DeiT, CLIP, and LLaVA), and downstream tasks (image classification and captioning), DetectViT substantially outperforms all baselines with as few as 64--128 OOD calibration samples, achieving a true positive rate of $100\%$ and a false positive rate of $0.17\%$ on BadCLIP. Deep neural networks are vulnerable to backdoor attacks, in which adversaries manipulate model predictions by injecting poisoned samples into training data. Detecting these samples remains challenging because legitimate semantic variation can obscure poisoning-related signals in learned representations. Consequently, class-level statistics used by existing detectors may flag benign feature deviations while overlooking poisoned samples that blend into the class distribution. "I Don't Think It's a Scam": A First Look at Family Intervention Barriers in Elder Abuse Discussions on Reddit and Baidu Tieba
Yipeng Wang, Huy Gia Han Vu, Jiaming Liu, Mihika Mehta, Poojitha Thota, Shirin Nilizadeh, Mohit Singhal
cs.SI · cs.CR · cs.CY
Abstract
When older adults trust scammers despite warnings, families face obstacles to intervention. Complainants aged 60 and older reported \$4.9 billion in losses in 2024 to the U.S. Internet Crime Complaint Center. To investigate family intervention barriers to elder scams, we collected 2M Reddit posts from May 2021 to June 2026 and 2B Baidu Tieba posts from 2007 to 2026. The final corpora contain 13,082 Reddit posts and 3,933 Baidu Tieba posts, labeled using platform-specific codebooks, manual reference annotations, and LLM coding. Through a mixed-methods analysis, we find that scams often extend beyond a single incident and are reported alongside debt problems and broken family relationships. In 68.0\% of Reddit posts recording reactions, older adults showed resistance or continued involvement; in Baidu Tieba family-confrontation posts, 41.9\% showed continued belief. Relatives identified fraud in 74.4\% of Reddit posts and narrated cases on Baidu Tieba, but without the victim's consent, relatives may lack the legal authority to intervene. In Reddit posts recording reactions, account locks or credential changes appeared in 8.9\% under resistance or continued involvement, compared with 33.3\% under acceptance. Measures such as phone or network monitoring and financial takeover were reported more often under resistance. Recovering funds is very limited in posts recording follow-up results of fraud; Baidu Tieba users reported that police classified older adults' voluntary transfers as civil disputes.

Superspecial curves of genus two over prime fields: Frobenius types and rational (2,2)-kernels
Hung Dang
math.NT · cs.CR · math.AG
Abstract
Superspecial curves of genus two over a prime field $\mathbb{F}_p$, and the rational $(2,2)$-isogenies between their Jacobians, are the vertices and edges of the graph on which genus-two isogeny-based cryptography is built. Let $C$ be such a curve, with Jacobian $J$ and Frobenius endomorphism $π$. We show that $π^2 = p\,α_*$ for a unique automorphism $α$ of $C$ over $\mathbb{F}_p$ whose action on the Weierstrass points is the square of that of Frobenius. For $p \ge 7$ this gives the list of Frobenius types of the Weierstrass points: eight types, each with its Weil polynomial, a congruence condition on $p$, and its number 15, 3, 3, 7, 1, 1, 3 or 1 of $\mathbb{F}_p$-rational $(2,2)$-kernels; when all Weierstrass points are rational, the 2-Tate pairing on $J[2]$ is determined by $p \bmod 8$. We then prove closed formulas, in terms of class numbers of imaginary quadratic orders and of $ζ_{\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt p)}(-1)$, for the mass of the curves of each type and for the mass of the rational kernels whose quotient is a product of elliptic curves. For $π^2 = \pm p$ the total masses are due to Ibukiyama and to Xue and Yu; our proofs use the 2-adic Tate modules, the symmetry of the Richelot correspondence and Eichler's mass formula, and, for the other curves, modules over orders of a quartic CM field. The kernels are counted through gluings of supersingular elliptic curves. As a consequence, the proportion of rational kernels with decomposed quotient is of order $p^{-1/2}(1+L(1,χ))$, where $χ$ is the quadratic character of $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-p})$. All formulas agree with an exact enumeration for the 37 primes $7 \le p \le 173$. Finally we describe the graph of $\mathbb{F}_p$-rational Richelot isogenies, which is far from connected in the range computed, and discuss what these results say about its use in isogeny-based cryptography.
